title: All of Annabel Crabb's desserts from the latest season of Kitchen Cabinet
text:
As the host of ABC iview’s Kitchen Cabinet for more than a decade, Annabel Crabb has made a habit of discussing politics at the dinner table.

Over that time, Annabel has also received well-earned praise for her show-stopping desserts and baked treats.

On the most recent season, which wrapped last week, Annabel indulged the sweet tooth of six very different members of Australia's 48th Parliament, whipping up everything from Guinness cakes and homemade wagon wheels to a vegan lemon poppyseed cake.

Read on if you're keen to sink your own teeth into all of the dessert recipes seen on the 2026 season.

These chunky homemade wagon wheels are given a flavour boost by the inclusion of a hint of nutmeg. (ABC TV)

This home-baked rendition of the classic chocolate-coated, marshmallow-filled biscuit treat is chunkier — and superior — to its store-bought counterpart.

The magical extra ingredient? Just a hint of nutmeg.

The coffee-scented cream-cheese frosting makes the cakes resemble tiny versions of a frothy glass of stout. (ABC TV)

A sweet, baked dessert made with beer might sound weird, but this moist, dark cake has an almost earthy richness and is perfect for those who don't love their desserts super sweet.

The decadent coffee-scented cream-cheese frosting makes these cakes look like tiny, well-poured pints of stout.

This moist lemon poppy cake is deliciously lemony and simple to make and no-one will believe it doesn’t contain eggs or butter. (ABC TV)

If you're sceptical about vegan cakes, this may be the one that changes your opinion.

It's incredibly simple to make, deliciously lemony and moist, and nobody will believe it doesn't contain eggs or butter.

Vermicelli pudding is often eaten in the morning at Eid, but it also makes a tasty dessert. (ABC TV)

Traditionally eaten in the morning in Eid, this Pakistani dish also makes a delicious dessert.

Fine strands of wheat vermicelli are toasted in ghee, then gently cooked with milk, sugar and cardamom until it thickens into a pudding. Highly addictive.

The tart has a no-bake white chocolate and cream cheese filling. (ABC TV)

This decadent tart has a chocolate and hazelnut crust, no-bake white chocolate and cream cheese filling and is ready in only 30 minutes.

The addition of thyme and burnt honey makes for a unique flavour combination and it's finished with dark berries and edible flowers.

These mini apple tarts use store-bought puff pastry, making them a quick and easy dessert option. (ABC News: Madeleine Hawcroft)

Incorporating the unbeatable combination of apple, cinnamon, butter and brown sugar, these little apple tarts are simple to make but a spectacular addition to the dinner table.

They use store-bought puff pastry and the red apple slices look like the petals of a rose.

title: Charles Perrottet denies being 'on board the money train' of developer
text:
The brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet has been accused of lying to the state's corruption watchdog over his dealings with fugitive property developer Jean Nassif.

Charles Perrottet is giving evidence for a second day at a NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) inquiry, which is examining whether he used his Liberal Party connections to advance Mr Nassif's business interests.

The commission previously heard allegations that money from Mr Nassif's company, Toplace, was channelled through companies linked to Liberal Party figures before being distributed to Mr Perrottet and others.

It is alleged Mr Perrottet, and lobbyists Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood expected to receive a combined $2 million from Mr Nassif.

Mr Perrottet denied lying to the inquiry. (ABC News)

Counsel assisting the commission, Peggy Dwyer SC, challenged Mr Perrottet on Monday over different explanations he had given the ICAC about messages he sent to Mr Nassif about Liberal Party preselection's.

Mr Perrottet told the public inquiry he mentioned preselection's to encourage Mr Nassif to pay money owed to Beckington, a lobbying firm run by Mr Ellis and Mr Greenwood — both of whom are key figures in the inquiry.

In a previous private hearing, Mr Perrottet said he was instead seeking a statutory declaration from Mr Nassif about alleged support for property developers in the Hills area.

Dr Dwyer accused Mr Perrottet of changing his story when confronted with the evidence.

"The great truism about telling a lie Mr Perrottet, is you have to be really good at remembering it," Dr Dwyer said.

Mr Perrottet rejected the accusation, saying both accounts could be true.

Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif is a key figure in the inquiry. (Background Briefing: Cherine Yazbeck, file photo)

Dominic Perrottet, who referred the allegations to ICAC in 2022, is not accused of wrongdoing.

'Tying yourself in knots'

The commission also examined messages in which Charles Perrottet told Mr Nassif he would make calls and approach people about one of the developer's projects.

Mr Perrottet said the person he claimed to be contacting did not exist.

"Ultimately, I made it up," Mr Perrottet told the inquiry.

"At times I would add my own political flavour to it [messages for Mr Nassif] to keep him on side."

Mr Perrottet's wife Anita spent last week being quizzed by the ICAC. (ABC News)

On Friday, Mr Perrottet said he wanted to appease Mr Nassif and would update him on Liberal Party affairs because he had an ulterior motive to seek some information from him.

Dr Dwyer accused Mr Perrottet of attempting to explain away messages that appeared to show him seeking money from the developer.

"Mr Perrottet, you are tying yourself in knots to get around obvious messages about you picking up money from Mr Nassif. Is that what's happening?"

Mr Perrottet said he disagreed with the suggestion.

'On board the money train'

The inquiry was also shown a message Mr Perrottet sent Mr Ellis in which he described an alleged system for developers to support the party faction while avoiding donation law restrictions.

Under NSW law, property developers and anyone donating on their behalf are prohibited from making political donations.

Mr Perrottet referred to it as the "money train," claiming developers could allegedly use cash or monthly government relations retainers instead of direct political donations.

Ms Dwyer spent the better part of Monday morning grilling Mr Perrottet on his evidence. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

Mr Perrottet claimed such retainers could be worth $50,000 per month.

Dr Dwyer then suggested Mr Perrottet wanted to establish a similar arrangement to benefit a Liberal Party right-wing faction.

"You wanted to get on board the money train, didn't you?" Dr Dwyer asked.

Mr Perrottet disagreed.

$148,000 cheque to Beckington

Mr Perrottet was also questioned about a meeting at the Longueville Hotel in Sydney's lower north shore involving Toplace lawyer Sharangan Maheswaran, Mr Greenwood and Mr Ellis.

He said he remembered a cheque being handed to one of his associates but initially said he did not know its value.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

The commission then showed him a photograph taken on his phone the following morning of an envelope addressed to Beckington with $148,000 written on it.

Dr Dwyer questioned why he would photograph the cheque the next morning if it had already been handed over at the pub.

"You are correct, I'm obviously mistaken," Mr Perrottet suggested.

He later suggested he may have instead delivered the cheque to Mr Greenwood's home.

Mr Perrottet has told the inquiry he was gathering evidence about alleged political activity involving developers while also helping his Liberal allies pursue unpaid bills.

title: Workplace watchdog finds 44 safety breaches across NSW farming sector
text:
The workplace safety watchdog has identified dozens of safety issues across labour-hire firms operating on New South Wales fruit farms in the wake of serious modern slavery allegations in the fruit-picking industry.

SafeWork NSW has issued 44 notices to labour-hire companies following inspections in the horticultural sector across the Coffs Harbour and Riverina regions.

Five prohibition notices were issued to Coffs Coast operators after SafeWork NSW identified serious safety risks at certain sites. The notices resulted in an immediate stop work until those risks are addressed and rectified.

The blitz comes after a report delivered by a state parliamentary inquiry into modern slavery that sparked serious concern about practices in the fruit-picking industry, with allegations that workers were being underpaid and were not being given appropriate entitlements.

In the Coffs Harbour region, inspectors spent eight days visiting 28 businesses and issued 34 compliance notices, which included 29 improvement notices and five prohibition notices.

In the Riverina, SafeWork worked with the State Insurance Regulatory Authority (SIRA) on a two-day operation during which another 32 businesses were inspected, and 10 compliance notices were issued.

SafeWork NSW has issued 44 breaches after conducting inspections on the Coffs Coast and Riverina. (ABC: Kim Honan)

SIRA officers verified workers' compensation coverage, including declared wages and worker classifications.

SafeWork NSW commissioner Janet Schorer said the blitz focused on pack houses, agricultural businesses and farms that were working in berry picking.

"We're interested in the labour hire arrangements, as well as the supply chain arrangements that happen in those particular industries," Ms Schorer said.

" What we saw in those locations and around the improvement notices was a range of issues with moving plant machinery, with electrical safety and with hazardous chemicals, which happens quite frequently in this industry. "

Ms Schorer said SafeWork NSW spent time talking with staff and employers about worker rights, safety systems and the available support systems.

She added that SafeWork NSW was training inspectors to recognise signs of modern slavery.

Janet Schorer lists the 44 safety notices that were issued on farms in the Riverina and Coffs Coast regions. (ABC News )

Ms Schorer said inspectors gave the farms instructions on what needed to be done to address the issues identified.

The inspector will also provide a time frame for changes to be made, and will visit again to ensure compliance.

SafeWork NSW had passed on any relevant information to the Australian Federal Police following the operation.

Ms Schorer said more operations would be conducted across the picking season.

'They will be found out'

NSW Work Health and Safety Minister Sophie Cotsis said there were "dodgy operators" out there that needed to be dealt with, but she conceded that there was more work to do.

"Labour hire operators who are not following work health and safety are doing the wrong thing, and they will be found out," Ms Cotsis said.

Sophie Cotsis has revealed SafeWork NSW issued 44 breaches to farms in the Riverina and Coffs Coast areas. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi )

She added that federal and state operators were working together to address issues in the berry picking industry because a "coordinated approach" was key.

"A number of these workers are very scared about providing information," Ms Cotsis said.

"I recently spoke to the Migrant Worker Centre that the government established, are doing really important work getting out into the communities.



"Getting the information out to these workers is very challenging. You can't just pick up a phone and talk to them; they're very scared, and they don't want to be identified."

Ms Cotsis said the NSW government was in favour of a national labour hire scheme, but some states had pulled out already.

She said that in NSW, the government was looking at a number of options so it could have its own scheme.

"We want to make sure workers go to work safely, are working safely, and come home to their family and friends safely," she said.

In addition to this, she said the government had increased the number of SafeWork inspectors.

title: Drilling company says 'exciting time' as gold and exploration hit highs
text:
A gold rush is being reflected in figures released today by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) that show $1.57 billion spent on exploration in Western Australia alone.

It comes after the Australian dollar gold price hit an all-time high of $7,688/oz in January. Earlier today it was trading at $6,236/oz.

The figure represents a decent increase on the 24/25 financial year of $1.03 billion.

In WA's gold heartland, one drilling company in particular is experiencing "unprecedented demand" amid an ongoing boom in mineral exploration.

The fortunes of the Kalgoorlie-based Topdrill have risen alongside metal prices and today it ranks among Australia's biggest drilling contractors, with more than 550 workers on its payroll.

Tim Topham hates the word "boom", but there's no doubt about the level of demand. (Supplied: Topdrill)

Founder Tim Topham, who started 20 years ago with a single drill rig and two employees, is set to take delivery of a 43rd drill rig in coming weeks.

"We're seeing the flow-on effects of Trump's behaviours and the gold price boom — it's something that's very real," he said.

"I hate the word 'boom', but this period of buoyancy has been really elevated. It's a pretty exciting time."

Signs pointing to the location of a working drill rig are a constant reminder of increased exploration activity in the Goldfields. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Working through holidays

The ABS data shows the bulk of Australia's investment in mineral exploration is being directed towards gold, with $1.93 billion out of a total of $4.27 billion dedicated to the search in the 2025-26 financial year.

In WA gold represented $1.57 billion of its total $2.99 billion spend on mineral exploration, including a record $461.1 million spent on exploration in the June quarter.

Mr Topham said gold exploration accounted for 95 per cent of Topdrill's workload.

A crew of exploration drillers after working on a hole in WA's Murchison that reached a depth of more than a kilometre. (Supplied: Topdrill)

"This is a period of unprecedented demand," he said.

"Historically there would be no work over the Christmas period and you would start to wind back into it by about February.

"The last two to three years we've seen a total change in that behaviour, so now we're drilling right through Christmas and New Year."

Impact of tax changes

While the expenditure figures show exploration is booming, the Association of Mining and Exploration Companies (AMEC) is concerned about proposed reforms to capital gains tax.

AMEC chief executive Warren Pearce said the federal government's changes would see more investment flow overseas and greenfields exploration in Australia "dry up".

Warren Pearce is concerned about capital gains tax changes impacting investment in the exploration sector. (ABC News: Phil Hemingway)

He said the sector relied heavily on retail investors and that when companies needed to raise capital again the investors would not be there.

Madeleine King says the government has invested heavily in the industry. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King said the government had invested heavily in Geoscience Australia and critical minerals.

"I would say no government in Australia has ever done more for the resources sector … I think exploration is in a very good space in Australia," she said.

Drill rig offsider Adrian Parise working in bushland near Widgiemooltha in WA's Goldfields. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

When times are tough

Exploration is booming now, but business owners such as Mr Topham have one eye on the present and the other on the horizon.

In the past, Topdrill has agreed to work for shares instead of cash under what are known as drilling-for-equity arrangements.

It can be incredibly lucrative if a discovery is made, but that is not the only reason Topdrill will accept shares in a company instead of cash.

A drill rig tests for gold about 25km east of Kalgoorlie-Boulder. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"It's a tool we've engaged with to keep our rigs busy when the market has changed," Mr Topham said.

"The traditional model is to lay staff off in those tougher times, so drilling-for-equity has been an important to keep the rigs spinning and we've been involved in some great discoveries through that initiative."

title: SA premier defends MotoGP tree removals with almost 400 now slated for chop
text:
SA Premier Peter Malinaukas has rejected claims he misled the public over the number of trees to be felled in Adelaide's east parklands to make way for a new city motorsport track.

Plans for the 4.13-kilometre circuit were released by the state government on Sunday, and will require new track to be laid in Victoria Park, cutting through the parklands between Wakefield Road and Rundle Road.

The project means 400 trees will be removed, including 42 significant trees and follows almost 600 trees being removed to make way for the North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment.

Opposition Leader Ashton Hurn said while the Liberals supported the government securing the MotoGP event, it was concerned about transparency before the state election.

She said it was "somewhat true" the premier had won a mandate for the project but it was "worthwhile reflecting as to whether people would have changed their vote if they knew it was 400 trees".

Ashton Hurn has questioned the government's transparency around the new Adelaide circuit. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

"Before the election we had the premier saying that it would be about 45 trees and now we know that that number has increased tenfold to 400," Ms Hurn said.

Mr Malinauskas denied he was misleading the public with his original claim.

"I simply recited what I was being told, and then we made clear that 45 number was significant trees, and of course now it's 42 significant trees on the plan," he said.

Differing views on environmental impact

When the premier first announced the MotoGP was coming to Adelaide from Phillip Island, he said the number of trees to be removed sat "at around about 45".

Premier Peter Malinauskas says the circuit redesign would see 42 significant trees felled. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

That later became almost 400 trees, including at least 42 significant trees. Another 88 other trees will be relocated.

The premier said commissioned arborists considered those to be ones that "we can safely move without being at great risk to those trees".

For every removal, the government has said it will plant 10 more, some of which are "mature stock".

Greens MLC Melanie Selwood said the proposal would mean almost 900 trees would be removed as part of works for both the motorsport track and the North Adelaide Golf Course upgrade.

"We shouldn't be cutting down any significant trees in the middle of a climate crisis," Ms Selwood said.

"The trees are precious to so many people here in South Australia and the premier just has total disregard for what those trees mean to people."

President of the Adelaide Parklands Association Mat Monti said the organisation would continue to oppose the action, including relocating yellow ribbons tied to trees along Dequetteville Terrace to those that now slated for removal.

Mat Monti of the Adelaide Park Lands Association has led environmental protests against the MotoGP project. (ABC News: Sarah Maunder)

They were critical of the length of the compulsory three-week public consultation, but have encouraged supporters to participate.

"What we're hoping and what we're calling on the government to do is listen to this consultation," they said.

"If the consultation is overwhelmingly negative, it might be time that the state government paused and actually thought about whether they're doing the right thing."

The government has attached $15 million in funding projects to what it has called "nature positive" upgrades for the parklands, a plan formulated with the Conservation Council of SA.

The peak environment organisation opposed the removal of trees but proposed actions to the government to lessen the environmental impact.

"I've not seen in my history this level of investment, particularly in nature and biodiversity outcomes within our cityscape of this scale. 15 million [dollars] is incredible," said its CEO Kirsty Bevan.

"I'm still deeply saddened by the loss of 42 significant trees which is going to change the look of our parklands absolutely."

A map showing the trees slated for removal (in red) from the proposed new Adelaide circuit. (Supplied: SA Government)

Concerns about cost and track plans

Bob Barnard, the designer of the original track used for Formula One racing in the 80s and 90s, previously suggested the new circuit would cost in the vicinity of $100 million.

Ms Hurn said that prediction had now proven accurate, with the track modification now costed at $96 million.

"The premier rejected that but we know that that's what South Australians will be forking out for the circuit alone," she said.

Costs for a new temporary pit building are yet to be confirmed.

Mr Barnard also designed the Phillip Island Grand Prix circuit, which will lose MotoGP to Adelaide from next year.

He was critical of the new project, particularly the suggestion of the new track being labelled a street circuit.

"The original Formula One track was a street circuit, you can't run a motorcycle track on a street circuit," Mr Barnard said.

" This is a normal track that's built within the parklands, so you can call it what you like, but it's not a street track. "

Around a third of the proposed track uses existing streets Rundle Road, Dequetteville Terrace and a segment of East Terrace, with the remainder to utilise new or existing track built on the Parklands.

The chief executive of the SA Motor Sport Board Mark Warren is appearing before a parliamentary committee today.

title: Ex-Carlton coach Voss gives assessment of Blues' finals hopes
text:
Michael Voss has stopped short of declaring Carlton a genuine premiership threat but sees no reason his former team cannot make a deep run in the finals.

The Blues are riding a wave of momentum under Josh Fraser, who has engineered a remarkable turnaround since taking the coaching reins when Voss stepped down in May.

Fraser has won 11 of 14 matches at the helm, capped off by the come-from-behind victory over Melbourne in last week's wildcard encounter.

The staggering run has optimistic Carlton fans daring to dream of a first premiership since 1995, ahead of an elimination final against Geelong at the MCG on Friday night.

But with another three wins required in sudden-death matches just to reach the grand final, Voss said a drought-breaking flag was most likely beyond the Blues this year.

"It's very hard, isn't it? Percentages say that's a tough gig," Voss said.

"But they're certainly playing a high level of football if you look over the course of the last 10 or 11 weeks.

"They're the equal-form team of the competition, so there should be no reason that they can't look at every game and say that it's winnable."

The Blues ended the Demons' season last Saturday night. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Voss fell on his sword at Carlton after a 1-8 (win-loss record) start to the season and is determined to look forward rather than back at what might have been.

He said Fraser was "doing a great job" as coach and results showed "the right decision has been made" in appointing the former Collingwood ruck as Blues coach.

Voss lauded captain Patrick Cripps and leaders of the playing group for their efforts in turning Carlton's season around.

"One of my last messages with the leaders was: 'It's over to you and how do you make this a really player-led group?'" Voss said.

"They've clearly done that and more numbers are coming with them, so the heavy lifting isn't just on a few.

"You've got a lot of people responding and there's some pretty incredible human beings amongst that group.

"I'm just really pleased that they're getting the rewards that they've obviously been working really hard for."

Voss says Carlton in a better place than when he took charge Michael Voss has struck a defiant tone after leaving Carlton, insistent the AFL club is in better shape than when he started as coach.

Carlton has won three of its past four meetings with Geelong, with Voss noting extra attention on key Cats duo Tom Stewart and Gryan Miers had served them well.

Voss said the Blues' work in the contested areas of the game would hold them in good stead.

"Where Geelong are underestimated quite a fair bit is their contested game," he said.

"They're not so much dominant when it comes to stoppages, but they are post-stoppage.

"Carlton can do that blindfolded and they showed that again on the weekend against Melbourne.

"When the whips were cracking they really ramped that part of the game up.

"Because they match up really well against that, they actually put themselves in a really good position to win games."

AAP

title: Queensland mum, Sydney dad among Australians missing in Nepal
text:
As rescue efforts continue along the Nepal-Tibet border following catastrophic floods, more Australian families are appealing for information about loved ones still missing in the region.

Sunshine Coast mother of two Renee Spry, who was on her way home from Nepal when flash flooding struck, is among the 43 Australians unaccounted-for.

Nepal flash floods updates: Follow this story as it unfolds with our live blog.

Ms Spry, aged in her early 50s, was one of several Australians who arrived at the Gyirong Port on the Nepal-Tibet border about 10 minutes before the disaster began.

Her sister, Clair Spry, said the disability support worker had just completed a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and was due to return home shortly after.

Renee Spry is one of 43 Australians missing after the deadly floods last week. (Supplied)

"Our beloved sister Renee is still missing from the Tibet-Nepal border after the devastating events from this week," her sister wrote on social media.

"We continue to pray for her, the Nepalese people and those also still [yet] to return to the safety [of] their homes and families."

Ms Spry's husband is trying to travel to Nepal to assist with the search for his wife.

Do you know more or are you affected? Tell us here.

Melbourne residents Sidharthi Kumari Sahu, 39, and her husband Sandeep Mohapatra, 43, have also been identified among the Australians missing in Nepal.

The couple from Wantirna South and four other Australians were part of a pilgrimage group with Kailash Journeys.

Sidharthi Kumari Sahu and Sandeep Mohapatra were among a group of pilgrims travelling in the region. (Supplied)

Close friend Rubila Rath told the ABC their loved ones still held hope that they would be found soon.

"They were beautiful souls and we just want them back," she said.

"She was like a sister to me, and he was like my brother-in-law. I'm just holding on to hope that we'll see them both again soon."

The pair were photographed in Kathmandu on Tuesday, along with Queensland woman Kanagamah Sundrasan and Australian Royal Air Force member Karan Bhardwaj, along with two of his friends from Brisbane.

Sydney IT worker Gopi Krishna Naidu Agastya is also missing in Nepal.

His friend, Pavan Kurucheti, said the 45-year-old father of two was at an immigration building on the Gyirong border crossing when the flash flood hit.

Gopi Krishna Naidu Agastya was on a pilgrimage in Nepal when his family lost contact with him. (Supplied)

Mr Agastya was among Australians travelling with the Isha Foundation, a spiritual organisation that facilitates pilgrimages to the sacred region.

Many of the 43 Australians missing after the disaster were pilgrims trekking from Nepal into Tibet to visit Mount Kailash, a site revered by four different religions.

Mr Agastya's wife, children, family and friends are anxiously waiting for news of the Parramatta resident, Mr Kurucheti said, urging anyone with information to reach out.

Nepalis in Australia touched by flood tragedy

The pain of the tragedy unfolding is being felt by Nepalis in some of the most remote parts of Australia.

Madhu Banthee, a resident of Santa Teresa, a tiny town south-east of Alice Springs, said there were 400 to 500 Nepali people living in Central Australia and that four or five families in the region had been affected by the disaster, including himself.

Families in Alice Springs gathered to light candles and pray for Nepal on Sunday evening. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

He has not heard from his best friend and Nepali authorities believe more than 2,400 people are still missing.

More than 250 people attended a vigil to show support and solidarity for the Nepali community in Alice Springs last night.

"My own story, you know, I had my best mate who lives in Brisbane and he was there in Nepal," Mr Banthee said.

"He was alive just two hours before the flood … we didn't hear any messages after that flood.

"I can imagine the families who lost their immediate families there … so it's a very, very tough time."

Mandhu Banthee says he has not heard from his best friend since the flooding in Nepal. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Mr Banthee said he still had hope for people who were missing.

"We heard lots of stories about miracles … I'm just waiting [for] the miracles," he said.

Mr Banthee said some community members were keen to give hands-on support and that others were planning fundraisers to send money home.

Yesterday the Australian government announced it would increase its humanitarian assistance for Nepal to $8 million.

Assistant Foreign Minister Matt Thistlewaite said this funding would mostly go towards the supply of hygiene kits.

"There's a desperate need for these kits for people in the region and also solar lights," he said.

"Obviously all of the power and telecommunications infrastructure has been wiped out.

"So those kits are being put together, they'll be transported by the Australian Defence Force over the coming days."

If you want to help support the thousands affected by the crisis, the ABC is supporting the Emergency Action Alliance member charities and their local partners. You can find more information here.

title: 28,000 irrigators lose $1.5-billion Murray Darling class action
text:
The New South Wales Supreme Court has found in favour of the Murray-Darling Basin Authority (MDBA) in a long-running class action over river management.

The action, which sought damages of between $750 million and $1.5 billion, was brought on behalf of 28,000 irrigators from the central Murray region of southern NSW and the Goulburn Murray region of northern Victoria.

It claimed the MDBA mismanaged river operations, causing lower water allocations, a loss of profits and higher temporary water prices, which meant some farmers could not meet supply contracts.

But Justice Tim Faulkner found the MDBA had no duty of care to avoid pure economic loss to one group of people over another and ordered the plaintiffs to pay the defendant's costs.

'It's not a loss'

Southern Riverina Irrigators chief executive Sophie Balwin said the plaintiffs would consider the judgment and avenues to appeal against the decision.

"Look, it is pretty disappointing, but I guess what I would say to people is it's not a loss," she said.

" I guess we've got to just digest what's happened today, have a bit of a look at the judgment and then go from there. "

Sophie Baldwin says the case has highlighted transmission losses in overbank flows. (ABC News)

In handing down his findings, Justice Faulkner said the MDBA was the independent body responsible for implementing the water-sharing framework agreed to by the states, and that the Murray River system was to be operated in the "public interest".

He accepted the defendant's submission that having a duty to irrigators would distort its independent role in exercising the provisions of the agreement in sharing water between the states.

The justice also found that as water allocations to individual irrigators were determined by respective states, there was not a sufficient relationship between the MDBA and the plaintiffs for a duty of care to be owed.

The court has found the MDBA had no duty of care to one group of irrigators. (ABC News: Melinda Hayter)

Decisions in 'dynamic' river system

The case centred around over-bank flooding at the Barmah Choke, a narrow section of the Murray River between Tocumwal and Deniliquin in southern NSW, from 2017 to 2019.

The plaintiffs argued the MDBA failed to follow its own operating plan, and that over-bank transfers, which flooded the Barmah-Millewa forest, were unjustified and known by the MDBA to cause high transmission losses.

The defence argued that over-bank transfers were not "unprecedented" and were done to ensure there was sufficient water to meet supply in South Australia.

It said the decisions were guided by modelling and the "experience of the MDBA operations team".

During the hearing last year, counsel for the MDBA, Sophie Callan SC, said the lawsuit was the latest manifestation of a problem that had existed since Federation.

"Namely that the waters of the Murray are a scarce resource, subject to conflicting claims between those interested in the use and conservation of the waters," she told the court.

Justice Faulkner described the Murray system as "unpredictable and dynamic".

"The decisions made by the MDBA were made in the context of balancing the risk of a shortfall [in meeting water requirements to SA] and the risk of a spill [by sending too much water to Lake Victoria]," he said.

In regard to allegations of negligence, the justice found there was no breach of duty in the MDBA's reading of climate outlooks, operating plans, or in the delegation of water releases in 2017.

'A significant admission'

Ms Baldwin said the decision highlighted important points about river management.

"I think one of the key things that came out of the class action was the admission by the MDBA that when they go over bank, they waste between 36 and 41 per cent of the water volume," she said.

"That's a significant admission, and with the continued push to relax constraints and flood private and public land, effectively every time they do that they're going to waste that volume of water."

In a statement, the Murray Darling Basin Authority said it was reviewing the judgment in detail.

"As the matter remains subject to appeal rights, it would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage," it said.

title: WorkSafe probes CFA fleet safety after oldest fire truck turns 37
text:
WorkSafe Victoria is "making inquiries" into the Country Fire Authority's aging truck fleet after safety concerns were raised by a lobby group.

The CFA Volunteers Group (CFAVG) contacted the regulator in May with a request for an investigation into the CFA's single-cab tankers.

WorkSafe told the ABC that inspectors were making "ongoing inquiries to ensure health and safety risks are being adequately addressed".

Inspectors have already met with CFA authorities at their Melbourne headquarters and visited several brigades in regional Victoria.

The CFA, which has been contacted for comment, is reportedly providing information to WorkSafe and facilitating access to appliances and documentation.

CFAVG president John Houston said repeated calls for more funding and better equipment had fallen on deaf ears, which prompted the group to approach WorkSafe.

"We have to recognise these trucks are no longer fit for purpose and are no longer safe," Mr Houston said.

"We believe that these concerns deserve some kind of independent scrutiny. It seemed to be the only course of action we could get some response from."

Single-cab tankers 'outdated'

A single-cab tanker fits three crew members in the enclosed cab, while a modern dual-cab tanker has the capacity to accommodate a crew of up to six.

Mr Houston said the single-cab tankers were a health and safety risk to the volunteers who had to ride on the back of the truck and those in the cab, which lacked air conditioning.

The CFAVG said the backlog of "out-of-date" tankers had been growing steadily for the past decade.

Emergency Services Minister Paul Edbrooke acknowledged the tankers have a life span and said he was happy to meet with anyone who had "suggestions" for improvements.

"If the CFA chief officer wants to talk about how we maybe manage the fleet, I'm more than open to those discussions," he said during a visit to Euroa last week.

"Certainly, as a former CFA volunteer, the trucks that are there now are light years ahead of the trucks that I was driving around in under a former government."

A Victorian government spokesperson said the CFA was "stronger, better funded and better resourced under Labor, with more trucks, modern stations and the equipment they need".

"Labor has increased the CFA's funding year-on-year with a new truck rolling out at a rate of every four days and every CFA region receiving new infrastructure funding in the latest budget," they said.

The CFA does not provide clear figures on its rolling replacement program, but data provided by the CFAVG showed there were 225 new primary tankers registered to regional brigades between 2016 and 2025.

In the 10 years before that 453 new tankers were delivered.

There are about 1,400 primary tankers distributed across 1,209 regional and peri-urban brigades.

The Muckatah Brigade’s 37-year-old tanker is the oldest in CFA service. (Supplied: CFA Volunteers Group)

Those are different to brigade-owned tankers, which are purchased with the help of the state government. The primary tankers are CFA-owned and state government-funded and can be shuffled around brigades at the CFA's discretion.

It is not the first time the CFAVG has pushed for better equipment.

Earlier this year the CFAVG submitted a report to the bushfire inquiry that detailed issues ranging from poor funding to outdated tankers and equipment, volunteer retention, poor communication services, and poor roadside vegetation and fuel load management.

The oldest CFA tanker in service is the Muckatah Brigade's two-wheel drive, single-cab tanker, built in July 1989.

The 37-year-old tanker is 17 years past its nominal use-by date and Muckatah CFA captain Glen Hamson said its reliability was a matter of concern.

"Late last year we had an issue with the pump on our tanker, which essentially blew up and we had to put the tanker in for repairs," he said.

"We were essentially without the tanker for four or five months and had to use a spare tanker in that time."

The tanker is not used for strike team duties, which limits the brigade's involvement in wider firefighting efforts, and Mr Hamson said there was no clear timeline for its replacement.

"There's this talk it's at the top of the list to be replaced, but there's no time frame that's been clearly specified," he said.

"So that's frustrating."

title: GLP-1 drug prescribed to woman with eating disorder via telehealth
text:
Experts are calling for greater oversight of telehealth clinics after an online clinic prescribed injectable weight-loss medications to a patient with a history of anorexia nervosa.

Kate (not her real name) was last hospitalised in 2022, and since then had been managing her condition with a GP and wider healthcare team.

But late last year the 25-year-old heard about a class of drugs called GLP-1 receptor agonists from a colleague at work.

These drugs, sold under brand names Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro, can help with weight regulation and have a positive impact on chronic health conditions, reduce risk of obesity-related cancer and improve quality of life.

But health experts are concerned they can be used by people to fuel and maintain eating disorders, leading to serious nutritional deficits and complications including death.

Loading...

Shortly after researching the drugs, Kate said she was targeted on Instagram by an ad from a telehealth clinic, which the ABC has chosen not to name, and made an online appointment.

While direct advertising of prescription drugs to consumers is not allowed in Australia, weight-loss companies can run "disease awareness" campaigns suggesting potential patients contact a doctor.

These advertising campaigns have previously been criticised by health experts as "unethical" with the potential to lead to worse outcomes for people with eating disorders.

Weight-loss drug manufacturers under fire for 'unethical' ads The pharmaceutical giants behind GLP-1 drugs launched advertisements directing people towards their doctor for weight loss. Some experts warn this may affect public health messaging.

Kate said she was not screened for an eating disorder by her telehealth practitioner.

"I booked my initial consultation and after that appointment it was criminally easy to access the medications," she said.

Kate admitted she lied about her health details during the phone consultation and then told the clinic she was interested in using GLP-1 medications.

After having a blood test, she was prescribed the weight-loss drug during a second phone appointment.

'Urgent need' to regulate telehealth

In Australia, it is estimated more than 1.1 million people are living with an eating disorder, with women twice as likely as men to experience one.

Eating disorders are complex and potentially life-threatening mental illnesses in which people have an unhealthy relationship with food, eating, and/or body weight and shape.

Experts have previously raised concerns over the misuse of GLP-1 drugs and eating disorder risks, and called for increased screening.

But Sarah Trobe, clinical psychologist and national director of the National Eating Disorder Collaboration (NEDC), said screening for eating disorders "for the most part was not happening" and she was not surprised to hear Kate's story.

"We know that the eating disorder voice is seeking that; anorexia will try and get access to a GLP-1," she said.

"And we need to think about all people with eating disorders … and how we keep them safe in this process."

Sarah Trobe says more needs to be done to keep vulnerable people safe from harm. (Supplied)

In Australia, there are currently no endorsed national standards for virtual care, although the federal government has recently tasked a committee with developing some.

These standards are not expected to be introduced until the end of next year.

Independent member for Kooyong Monique Ryan, who worked as a paediatric neurologist and medical researcher prior to politics, said 2027 would be too late.

"There's an urgent need to regulate telehealth services in Australia more quickly and effectively," she said.

Last week, Dr Ryan wrote to Federal Health Minister Mark Butler, asking for an inquiry into telehealth services, which could cover prescribing-pattern oversight for high-risk medicine classes such as peptides, GLP-1 agonists, stimulants and medicinal cannabis.

Ozempic and eating disorder concerns prompt calls for more screening Health experts are concerned Ozempic and other GLP-1 agonist drugs may be inappropriately prescribed to people experiencing disordered eating.

In a statement to the ABC, she said commercial telehealth companies screened "inadequately for eating disorders" and bypassed "the normal GP relationship".

"They largely operate outside Medicare and the PBS, so there's no systemic data on what they're prescribing and their patient outcomes.

"There's no requirement on them to screen for eating disorders before prescribing GLP-1 weight loss drugs. And the fact that they dispense prescribed medications themselves is a conflict of interest which is illegal in other forms of medical care."

Mr Butler's office was contacted for comment, which passed the request on to the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing.

A department spokesperson pointed out that virtual care standards were in development, but did not respond to questions about an inquiry.

Not-for-profit advocacy group Patients Australia has its own set of telehealth standards, developed in collaboration with providers.

Do you know more about this story? Share it with us here.

'You're eating the wrong things'

In a subsequent phone appointment for a repeat script, Kate said she asked for the medication dose to be increased.

In response, she said the clinic asked about her food intake and exercise and provided advice that she said she found "forceful" and "intimidating".

"They basically said … you're eating the wrong things, you're eating too much," Kate said.

" Hearing that specifically in terms of my food was quite jarring for the eating disorder. "

Trevor Steward, an associate professor at the University of Melbourne and director of the Brain and Mental Health Hub, said conversations about eating disorders needed to be sensitive.

"Patients won't always raise their own history with an eating disorder without being prompted and it should be explored before deciding to begin taking these medications," he said.

The ABC contacted Kate's telehealth provider about their process for screening and how they protected patients from harm when prescribing weight-loss drugs, but did not receive a response.

A spokesperson for the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) said it expected all practitioners to undertake a comprehensive and holistic assessment of all patients to properly assess that any recommended or prescribed treatment was appropriate.

"This includes assessment of any increased potential for vulnerability before proceeding with treatments," the spokesperson said in a statement.

Experts have previously raised concerns over the misuse of GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Specifically in relation to weight-loss medications, the spokesperson said prescribers should consider whether patients had disordered eating, self-image or body image concerns.

"Practitioners should recognise that telehealth is not appropriate for all consultations as the lack of in-person interaction can limit the ability to provide safe and effective care," they said.

More education needed for GPs

Dr Trobe said telehealth prescribing might not be the best model for prescribing weight-loss medications.

"We can't have this low-touch model where people are having a phone call without adequate assessment, without sighting the individual and then no ongoing monitoring … to ensure this person is safe."

Kristi Griffiths, a senior research fellow at the InsideOut Institute at the University of Sydney, agreed that screening and evidence-based eating disorder care should be used when indicated.

"There also needs to be policy-level changes to online prescribing. For instance, requiring at a minimum a video call to help validate self-reported weight," Dr Griffiths said.

ABC Health in your Instagram feed Follow @abchealth on Instagram, where we're busting myths and sharing practical, smart health advice.

Separate to the standards in development, Dr Trobe said the NEDC was making recommendations to government about obesity management and treatment pathways, which she hoped would lead to safer prescribing of GLP-1 drugs.

These included prescribing by practitioners who were informed about the drugs and their usage and had kept up with the evidence, rather than by people who were "working outside the scope of their practice".

Kate has stopped using GLP-1 drugs with the help of her regular GP and is speaking out to help others.

"Knowing how easy it was to access for me and knowing how many people struggle with an eating disorder, it actually made me scared at the same time," she said.

Preeya Alexander is a practising GP and credentialed eating disorder clinician. She is working with the National Eating Disorders Collaboration (NEDC).

title: Debt-ridden property firm Bathla may collapse this week, says administrator
text:
Administrators of major property developer Bathla Group have warned that the business does not have enough money to survive until the end of this week unless it secures urgent funding to pay staff.

Some of the company's 350 staff have not been paid for eight weeks, administrators Teneo said in a press conference.

"We can't go to the end of the week if we don't have money for payroll on Thursday," Stephen Longley, Teneo's senior managing director, said.

"We don't have any cash to pay wages [and] we don't have any cash to pay suppliers.

The gates to Bathla Group's headquarters closed after it announced it had plunged into administration. (ABC News: Lin Lin)

"So unless that situation can be resolved, we won't have any other option but to close the business."

Administrators were appointed last Tuesday after Bathla was unable to pay debts that topped $3.2 billion.

On Thursday, administrators asked for a cash injection of $20 million to keep the business afloat.

The NSW government has declined to provide a lifeline but they are hopeful someone else might step forward.

Teneo also said it had borrowed $1 million from its own head office so Bathla Group could afford to pay for vehicle registrations, petrol and "just to keep the lights on".

"But that can't last," Mr Longley said.

Administrators say Bathla Group needs an urgent cash injection. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Bathla Group currently has more than 200 development projects across Sydney.

The administrators have said they will give priority to 45 of the projects that are already under construction and can be completed by February or March, if they secure more funding.

Those "will deliver somewhere between 2,000 and 2,500 homes. So that's really what we're focused on," Mr Longley said.

"The lenders are very keen for those sites to be finished, so I think subcontractors that are working on the sites will be looked after in time and will be paid," he added.

"We just need to get through this week to work out the funding arrangement to do that."

Artwork of townhouses that Bathla planned to build. (Supplied: Bathla)

Administrators are hoping a $20 million cash injection could keep Bathla going for another month to give them the chance to identify where the "real need" was into the future.

A "handful" of staff were stood down on Friday, and a review is underway to ascertain which ones are "mission critical" and which ones can be "let go".

That could affect Bathla's foreign workers who are on temporary visas, the administrator noted.

title: One dead, 15 missing after Grand Canyon flash flood
text:
One person has died and about 15 others remain missing or unaccounted-for after a flash flood in the Grand Canyon, the US National Park Service says.

The National Park Service said on Sunday evening, local time, that the body of a 46-year-old man had been recovered near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River.

The agency said coroners from the Coconino County Medical Examiner's Office had been sent to the scene.

The update came a day after floods hit the Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area, the service said, adding that it was working with Arizona authorities to evacuate people and account for missing individuals.

Torrents of water wiped out footbridges and significantly altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and creating what appeared to be a new river rapid.

Loading...

Earlier, the park service said that more than 20 people were believed missing.

As of Sunday morning, local time, 62 people had been evacuated, and others were scheduled to be evacuated, it said.

Evacuations continue

As the park service tries to account for everyone in the area, it is asking anyone with details about people hiking or camping there to make contact.

It said it was working with the Arizona Department of Public Safety to continue evacuations on Sunday.

"This is a reminder of what a dynamic and active landscape Grand Canyon is," said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University.

Remnants of stone bridge pylons along Bright Angel Creek following a flash flood that destroyed the footbridge. (AP: James Thompson/National Park Service)

Popular tourist spots including the Bright Angel Campground, Phantom Ranch and parts of the North Kaibab trail remained closed while park officials surveyed the damage, the park service said.

Because the main water line was out of service, starting on Monday, tourists will not be able to stay overnight at lodges and hotels within Grand Canyon National Park. Year-round residents are being asked to conserve water.

"These measures are crucial for ensuring the safety and sustainability of water resources," the park service said in a statement.

More than 60 people were evacuated from Phantom Ranch, which has a historic canteen and dorms, and is a common spot for rafters to get off and on the river.

Erica Viola said she was at Bright Angel Campground when the rain started on Saturday afternoon, and she and about 50 other hikers watched the creek rise and then debris start to flow by, including what looked like a bunkhouse.

Bright Angel Creek near the Phantom Ranger Station in the Grand Canyon after flash flooding. (AP: Parth Desai)

The group was taken by helicopter to safety, ending her adventure two days early, she said.

Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with a group of fellow physicians and a park ranger when the downpour started.

"We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere," he said.

Later, as they made their way toward Phantom Ranch, a colleague shouted "Up, Up, Up, Up!" as a 1-meter debris wall headed toward them and they ran up into a patch of cacti, he said.

They were rescued by helicopter that evening after reaching the Phantom Ranch area, he said.

A storm system moving across the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park on August 29. (AFP: J Baird/National Park Service)

About 1 to 2.5 centimetres of rain fell within 30 minutes in the rocky area, where there is a steep drop in elevation, said National Weather Service meteorologist Justin Johndrow in Flagstaff.

"Most of it ran off instantly," Mr Johndrow said.

He said the flooding happened on the north side of the Grand Canyon, where Bright Angel Creek comes from the North Rim down to the Colorado River 1,828 meters.

AFP/AP

title: Knight's prop cops season-ending ban after send-off
text:
Jacob Saifiti's NRL season is all but over after the Newcastle prop was handed a four-game suspension for a high tackle on Warriors winger Luke Laulilii.

Saifiti was sent off in the first half of Sunday's 46-32 defeat in Auckland and was handed a grade two reckless high tackle charge by the NRL's match review committee on Monday morning.

The Knights have a bye for the final round of the regular season, meaning Saifiti's ban will only kick in for their first finals game.

Newcastle — currently sitting seventh — will play an elimination final in week one but even if they were to upset the odds and qualify for the grand final, the Fijian prop would still be on the sidelines.

Saifiti's only hope of playing in the NRL again this season hinges on the prop contesting the charge at the judiciary on Tuesday in a bid to reduce his punishment.

Should the front-rower fight the suspension and lose his appeal, he will have another week added to his four-game ban.

Elsewhere, Cronulla prop Tom Hazelton is set to miss Cronulla's final regular season game against Melbourne after being cited for a hip-drop tackle on Ronald Volkman.

Hazelton was sin-binned by referee Ashley Klein late in Sunday's loss to Parramatta but will serve a one-game ban with an early guilty plea and be free to return for week one of the finals series.

title: Indigenous numbers in the AFL are down, but there's talent in the Top End
text:
A couple of years ago Hawthorn's Kaitlyn Ashmore, a Dja Dja Wurrung woman, spent some time in Alice Springs.

She was immediately taken by the gift for footy so many kids had up there, but knew the pathways for development were limited.

"I've been out to the communities … the talent up there is incredible," Ashmore said on the eve of the AFLW's Indigenous Round.

"But it's just getting them down here, or getting them in a program, and then keeping them in there and making them feel culturally safe."

Loading Instagram content

She was in the Red Centre in support of the Dreamtime Academy, an initiative founded by AFLW player Lulu Pullar along with fellow First Nations players Courtney Hodder, a Badimaya and Whadjuk woman, and Ally Anderson, a Ghungalu and Wakka Wakka woman.

There are 22 Indigenous players listed across the AFLW competition, down from 26 in 2023. In the men's competition the number has dropped from 87 in 2020 to 62 this season.

Ashmore said that was why the Indigenous Round was so important.

"It's honestly representation," she said.

"If we keep doing that, and celebrating Indigenous people, culture and stories like that, then hopefully we can get some more girls that want to join us."

'Work to do': AFL targets Indigenous player boost The AFL is considering a range of measures to boost the number of Indigenous players in the league following a significant decline in recent seasons.

On Sunday night more than 4,000 people packed out the stands at Marrara Stadium to watch Richmond beat Essendon in the Dreamtime match.

Among the spectators were diehard Tigers and Bombers fans and some who had never seen an AFL game before.

Last year the marquee Indigenous Round match was on a Friday night in Darwin and attracted almost 6,000 people.

But the game was fixtured around the men's wildcard round on a day with six AFLW matches and many locals said Sunday's 6:50pm time slot may have led to lower attendance than last year.

Richmond beat Essendon in front of a 4,000-strong crowd in Darwin. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

Match gets young fans dreaming

The elite game in the Top End was one part of nurturing football in the Northern Territory and helping to grow grassroots participation.

Top End Youth Academy head coach Ben White said just a couple of years ago most kids did not have an answer when he asked who their favourite AFLW player was.

He said now they were naming players such as Richmond's Monique Conti and Sydney's Zippy Fish.

"We've got those figureheads of the AFLW that girls can look up to and see that pathway. It's amazing," White said, crediting the Dreamtime match for bringing the game closer to community.

The crowd in Darwin for the Dreamtime game was a mix of diehard footy fans and new supporters. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

This has also been helped by the recent Northern Territory inclusions to the AFLW of Annabel Kievit, who plays for the Gold Coast Suns, and Dom Carbone, who was elevated to Collingwood's senior list for this season after playing for the Darwin Buffettes.

Essendon captain Bonnie Toogood said one of the most pleasing parts of coming up to the Top End with the Bombers was seeing the next generation of Indigenous kids in the stands.

Essendon has a strong connection with the Tiwi Islands. In April this year, AFLW players Mia Busch and Amy Gaylor, alongside The Long Walk's Jack Peris, ran footy clinics across the Tiwi Islands and West Arnhem Land.

Bonnie Toogood (right) says the Dreamtime game in Darwin is special for the players and competition. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

The Essendon players and staff will visit schools in Darwin on Monday.

Toogood said it was important to the team to connect with the community.

"It's the main reason as to why we want to come up here and celebrate Dreamtime," she said.

The Top End Youth Academy is fostering young talent and aiming to improve the standard of the game in the NT. (AFLNT Media: Tymunna Clements)

AFLNT launched the Darwin-based Top End Youth Academy this year in response to years of community demand for development opportunities and to strengthen existing talent pathways.

In a matter of months more than 400 players attended academy trials and more than 270 participants were picked up.

Youth Academy manager Josh Kleine was not surprised by the interest.

"Where those numbers might be higher than we expected, it doesn't shock me because there is that love and passion for the game up here," he said.

The AFLW has shown young kids that there is a pathway to the elite level. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

Kleine said there were a few times during the trials when he and White looked at each other and thought "we've got a fair bit of work to do here'".

But within a matter of months the skills of the kids, aged 10-15, improved out of sight.

"We were actually sitting here in this room and watching them do their warm up and they're just kicking in lanes, getting ready for the game, and nearly every target was being hit," Kleine said.

"We've done some work on things like leg drives and different things. And to see someone who was struggling to get the concept, panicked a little bit, and sort of rushed handballs out, to see that then translate into a game where they're actually taking the tackler on and driving through the contest, it's amazing to see.

"They're the moments that really get you. When you've had that time with the kids and you're coaching them, and you see those things where it's a kid who might have been struggling in this area, you put in the time on the track and then you see it translate on the field.

"It's those little moments that you find really touching."

There are more than 270 players in the Top End Youth Academy. (AFLNT Media: Tymunna Clements)

Kleine said the Darwin kids had a bit more access to programs and competitions than those in other parts of the NT, but the plan was for the academy to expand to places such as Tiwi, Katherine and Alice Springs.

"One thing with our academy [that] we always talk about is, we've only got you for an hour and a half a week on the track with training … we're limited with the time we have," he said.

"So our encouragement is take the lessons we teach you and do the work away from on during the week as well.

"And the girls, the work they're putting in on the track, you're definitely seeing it. You can see when they come back the next week — they've gone away and they've worked on these things. They've done their extra 100 kicks or whatever it is."

Documentary follows young Indigenous women chasing AFLW dreams Arthurina Moreen's desire was so great to play footy, she'd practice kicking bottles with her bare foot. A new documentary has shone a light on her resilience, and that of three other Tiwi Islander women as they chase AFLW stardom.

Kleine said he hoped to see more local talent make it to the elite level, but the goal was also to strengthen the game in the NT.

"Ultimately, not everyone's going to make it, but we're creating stronger territory football off the back of it," he said.

"Half our kids, we hope they become the future captains, the future coaches, all those sorts of things, and that the local clubs are here in the next 15 years.

"It's a flow-and-effect to make Territory footy stronger in the long run … it is a tumbleweed-type thing, where it just flows on, and everyone's continually growing and improving.

"Hopefully it helps close those gaps."

title: 'Outdated' law costing teens $411m a year in superannuation, modelling finds
text:
Thousands of teenage Victorian workers are missing out around $115 million in superannuation due to a law which excludes some under-18s from guaranteed super, according to new modelling.

The peak body representing profit-to-member superannuation funds, the Super Members Council, said under-18s were excluded from guaranteed super unless they worked more than 30 hours a week for one employer.

The council said its analysis found about 156,000 teen workers will miss out on an average of $735 in super in 2026-27, adding up to $115 million across the state.

Misha Schubert from the Super Members Council says currently the law discriminates against young people. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert said that figure was the highest of any state in Australia.

"Teenage workers in Victoria are being denied a basic workplace right that 17 million other working Australians enjoy — and that's just not fair," she said.

"A young person who earns a wage should also be paid super.

"Yet this outdated and discriminatory law treats teen workers differently just because of their age and their hours."

The Super Members Council says its analysis shows 156,000 young workers are missing out on super due to the law. (ABC Gippsland: Bec Symons)

The Super Members Council found young workers in NSW would miss out on $105 million, out of a nationwide total of $411 million in missed super this financial year.

Its analysis found 91 per cent of under-18s worked fewer than 30 hours a week.

It said the average teenage, part-time worker could miss out on $2,500 in super contributions by age 18, which could compounds to $11,000 by retirement.

The council is calling for the law to be scrapped and said it was "out of step with community expectations".

"Many teenagers have their first jobs in retail, hospitality, care and community services. These are real jobs, with real wages, and they should come with real super," Ms Schubert said.

Loading...

"The earliest super contributions matter because they have the longest time to compound.

" Missing out on hundreds or thousands of dollars as a teenager can mean losing much more by retirement. "

Labor members vote to extend compulsory super payments

A push to reform the law is being led federally by the Greens, which introduced an amendment bill into parliament earlier this month.

The party also secured a Senate inquiry on the issue, which will report to parliament in November.

"For too long, Australia's superannuation system has failed young workers. It's time for young workers to be paid the super they deserve," a Greens spokesperson said at the time.

"The continued exclusion of workers under 18 who work fewer than 30 hours per week is a clear case of legislated age-based discrimination that no longer has any defensible policy rationale."

Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers has expressed support for reform of superannuation laws affected under-18s. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers has previously expressed support for reform, saying it was an "important" issue, but is yet to make any legislative moves.

"We are always looking at ways to strengthen the superannuation system and make it deliver for more workers," he said in June.

Delegates at Labor's National Conference last month voted to include a policy to extend compulsory superannuation payments to under-18s, regardless of how many hours they worked.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said it was concerned by the push for reform, saying it would have "very serious consequences for the small business community and the broader business community".

title: Screen Queensland funding cut shakes film industry confidence
text:
A government funding cut to Queensland’s film and television sector could erode confidence in the industry and turn movie makers away from the Sunshine State.

Queensland Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek last week announced $50 million in incentives funding for government-owned agency Screen Queensland (SQ) over the next two years.

Lights, camera, action! Local and international filmmakers are choosing to make more films in North Queensland, so could Cairns be the next industry hotspot?

In real terms, that represents a funding cut for SQ, which was granted $42 million in incentives funding in the 2025-26 state budget, and $38 million per annum in the two budgets prior.

Screen Producers Australia chief executive Matthew Deaner said the cut confirmed industry fears that had been circling since the state budget was handed down.

"The Queensland government is significantly reducing the incentives that support the attraction of screen production, business and economic activity in the state," Mr Deaner said.

Screen Producers Australia CEO Matt Deaner says the funding cut could drive productions away from Queensland. (Supplied)

"Producers have chosen to locate their businesses in Queensland based on the stability and level of state investment.

"Our members indicate that New South Wales, Victoria, Western Australia and South Australia, as well as international production hubs, are now being considered for their business and production locations."

According to state government figures, SQ generated more than $541 million in "direct Queensland production expenditure" in the 2025-26 financial year and employed more than 6,600 people.

Mr Deaner said cutting SQ’s funding was a "relatively modest saving" that could cost the state "many times that amount in small-business and economic activity".

" The risk here is that it undermines Queensland's position as one of Australia's, if not the worlds', leading screen-production destinations. "

The state’s announcement also came as a shock to the City of Gold Coast, which has hosted production for Hollywood blockbusters Elvis, Aquaman, Thor: Ragnarok and others in recent years.

Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate is seeking clarification on funding levels from the state government. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

A spokesperson for the Gold Coast mayor said Tom Tate had asked Mr Langbroek for more details.

"We have written … seeking clarification on this funding and what other funding is coming from the state for the screen industry in 2026-27 and in the next financial year," the spokesperson said.

In a statement, SQ chief executive Jacqui Feeney said "rapid growth" in Queensland’s screen industry had been accompanied by "record-breaking demand for funding" in recent years.

"Screen Queensland is currently finalising changes to our incentive rates to balance momentum with sustainability across the sector," Ms Feeney said.

Screen Queensland CEO Jacqui Feeney says the agency is revising its incentive offerings to attract future productions. (Supplied: Screen Queensland)

"Our revised incentives will also still be offered in combination with the federal government’s 30 per cent offsets and rebates."

Mr Langbroek did not answer specific questions about how a reduction in funding could impact industry confidence in Queensland.

Nor did he answer questions about why SQ funding had been cut.

"The Crisafulli government is delivering multi-year funding certainty to the screen industry after Labor left the sector with no guarantees," Mr Langbroek said.

"Only with multi-year funding certainty can the industry forward plan and support a pipeline of projects across two years, creating more jobs for Queenslanders and boosting our local economy."

Macquarie Group has detailed interactions between its board member, former KPMG partner Michelle Hinchliffe, and KPMG executives during the tender process for its lucrative audit contract but did not indicate there was any wrongdoing on her part. KPMG was dumped as Macquarie’s preferred auditor last week following the revelations that emerged from the whistleblower scandal, in which senior audit partners accessed confidential client information to win new business. Michelle Hinchliffe was a long-time partner at KPMG before joining the BHP and Macquarie boards. Trevor Collens One of the whistleblower allegations was that the audit tender was compromised by KPMG involvement, including that of Hinchliffe, who left the firm to join Macquarie’s board in 2022. In response to questions from the Senate committee investigating the whistleblower scandal, Macquarie responded on Friday with details that include Hinchliffe meeting with the firm’s then chairman, Martin Sheppard, via her role as a BHP director.

She also socialised with other partners involved in the tender process. Related Article Consulting An email, a smiling emoji and the expulsion of a KPMG high-flyer “As a director and audit committee chair of three public companies operating in multiple jurisdictions, Michelle Hinchliffe frequently meets with representatives of professional services firms, including but not limited to KPMG,” Macquarie said in response to questions from the committee. She also met with KPMG partner Charles Hatchman for dinner with his wife but “Mrs Hatchman was unwell and unable to attend the dinner, but Mr Hatchman visited the restaurant briefly to excuse them both from dinner”, Macquarie said. Hinchliffe also had a meal with another KPMG partner, Patricia Stebbens, and met with various UK partners through other board roles.

Macquarie noted that the list was not exhaustive: “It is not practicable for her to maintain a comprehensive record of every contact, formal and informal, that she has with every person.” Hinchliffe also met with KPMG executives who were directly pitching for Macquarie’s business, but she did not vote on the matter due to potential conflicts over her previous role with KPMG. This masthead has asked Macquarie if it was satisfied with the responses provided by Hinchliffe. The bank has yet to respond. Macquarie chairman Glenn Stevens last year described concerns over Hinchliffe’s role in the audit tender – despite strong links to KPMG – as “silly talk”. But he dropped a bombshell at the Macquarie annual meeting at the end of July by announcing a review of KPMG’s ability to conduct the audit, and review of how it won the tender.

Great Southern Mining has struck shallow gold 200m north of its 100 per cent-owned Mon Ami project, 12km south of Laverton in Western Australia. The results raise the prospect of a northern extension to its 1.56-million-tonne resource grading 1.11 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for 55,500 ounces. The 10-hole, 1392m reverse-circulation (RC) campaign at the company’s Blanc Plat prospect was led by 14m at 1.05g/t gold from 36m, including 1m at 6.33g/t. Other hits included 7m at 0.7g/t from 70m, 3m at 1.07g/t from 38m and 6m at 0.66g/t from 108m. Great Southern Mining’s drill rig in action at the company’s Mon Ami gold project near Laverton in WA. Blanc Plat was already carrying some historical gold smoke, with earlier drilling returning 2m at 4.8g/t gold from 70m and 2m at 3.23g/t from 100m. Those hits support the company’s interpretation of a potential northern extension to Mon Ami. Almost 65 per cent of mineralisation above 0.2g/t in the latest campaign occurs in the oxide zone. The companyis targeting shallow oxide gold, which could enhance the economics of a small-scale mining operation. Supporting that view, previous metallurgical testwork at Mon Ami achieved average gold recoveries of about 95 per cent from oxide and transitional material using conventional processing methods.

Advertisement

‘These results highlight the significant potential for growth in the resource.’ Great Southern Mining managing director Matthew Keane Management says the combined results potentially open a second growth front north of Mon Ami. Blanc Plat lies on the gold-bearing Barnicoat Shear Zone, or a splay, with 200m between the two areas still largely untested. Cross-cutting structures may help concentrate gold along the regional shear, while mineralisation remains open another 425m north to the tenement boundary. The deeper growth case has already delivered some serious drill-bit encouragement. Earlier holes at Mon Ami returned 16m at 3.37g/t gold from 178m, featuring 4m at 8.54g/t and 2m at 6.86g/t, while other hits included 1m at 7.28g/t within a broader six-metre interval grading 1.83g/t from 150m and 16m at 1.28g/t from 281m. Another hole struck 19m at 1.12g/t from 213m, including separate one-metre sections going at 4g/t and 5g/t gold, extending Mon Ami mineralisation 55m down-plunge. The hole sits 140m southwest of recent Blanc Plat drilling, while the main Vertical Lode was pushed up to 60m down-dip, giving management growth potential beneath the resource and to the north. Great Southern Mining managing director Matthew Keane said: “While it is still early days at Blanc Plat, this target is showing signs of being a potential extension to the Mon Ami deposit, which could complement the existing resource.”

Advertisement

With the northern opportunity taking shape, the company will assess the latest RC results in geological context before planning follow-up infill and extensional drilling. Further mapping and surface geochemical sampling may also help constrain the Blanc Plat mineralised corridor. Blanc Plat and Mon Ami sit on a granted mining licence 12km east of Gold Fields’ Granny Smith processing facility. Great Southern considers Mon Ami a potential near-term development opportunity. The project already has plenty of its development ducks lined up, with archaeological, ethnographic, flora and fauna surveys, metallurgical and waste-rock studies completed and a haulage route to the sealed Elora-Mount Weld road granted. A cluster of nearby mills could potentially provide future satellite feed or toll-treatment options, should sufficient economic ounces be defined. Adding geological spice is the historic Ida H underground mine, 8km along the same regional shear. The old-timers reportedly produced 170,650 ounces of gold at an average grade of 22.6g/t, providing a high-grade example of what the structure has hosted elsewhere. Corporate interest around Laverton is also bubbling. Industrial Minerals recently completed its acquisition of Galleon Metals’ 15-licence, approximately 205-square-kilometre Laverton gold portfolio, providing another example of gold company positioning in the district.

Great Southern currently has plenty of other exploration bullets in the chamber. As Mon Ami grows deeper and with Blanc Plat pointing north, the immediate prize is closer to home.
