Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Lindian locks in early feed for Kazakh heavy rare earths plant Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright August 31, 2026 — 2:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In a savvy strategic move, Lindian Resources has executed an exclusive option to secure a substantial heavy rare earth minerals stockpile in Kazakhstan. The material could become a ready-made feed source for its recently acquired Summit Atom Rare Earth Company’s (SARECO) hydrometallurgical processing facility in the central Asian nation. The deal gives Lindian the right to acquire an initial 13,389 tonnes of previously extracted material from the Aktau stockpile, which contains the sought-after heavy rare earth elements dysprosium, terbium and yttrium. Lindian Resources’ recently acquired processing infrastructure within the SARECO mixed rare earths carbonate (MREC) facility. The move is a notable coup for Lindian and complements its massive Kangankunde light rare earth minerals project in Malawi, East Africa. It potentially fast-tracks the company’s entry into the lucrative heavy “magnet” rare earths market, which supplies the vital ingredients of high-powered magnets used in the construction of electric vehicles, power generation equipment and a growing range of advanced medical, electronic and defence technologies. SARECO was initially established as a high-level, multinational joint venture between two institutional giants, Kazatomprom and Sumitomo Corporation, to recover rare earth elements from uranium-derived residues, commissioning the Stepnogorsk facility in 2012. Ore material from Aktau was supplied to SARECO, making it directly relevant to Lindian’s evaluation of the opportunity today.

Advertisement

‘Aktau is strategically important because it was historically used as feedstock for SARECO.’ Lindian Resources executive director Zac Komur Years after commissioning, the original Kazatomprom-Sumitomo partnership dissolved due to severe feedstock constraints and a shift in corporate strategy. When the facility went dormant, the original founders ultimately sold the asset and transferred it out of their portfolios. Kazakhstan-based RA-Group LLP acquired the idle facility following the original founders’ exit. Rather than being a pioneer miner from 2012, RA Group acted as the local Kazakhstan entity which consolidated the asset’s land, warehouses and infrastructure. Lindian originally announced a joint venture framework with RA-Group in March 2026, under which it would acquire a 51% majority interest in the SARECO processing facility for an initial valuation. When the deal was first struck, RA-Group held the remaining 49% interest in the incorporated joint venture alongside Lindian’s 51 per cent. Following extensive due diligence, Lindian shifted strategy to secure 100 per cent ownership of the SARECO facility in early August, a move which strongly reflected the broader opportunity Lindian had identified at SARECO. RA-Group LLP negotiated a substantial exit package, becoming the direct recipient of up to US$22 million (A$30.72M) in Lindian equity, comprising US$15 million (A$20.94M) in fully paid ordinary shares and US$7 million (A$9.77M) in milestone-driven performance rights.

Advertisement

Under the terms of its latest agreement with SARECO, Lindian has nailed down the option over the initial stockpile, with no upfront cash consideration payable. The company says 7549 tonnes of the material have already been identified as ready for transport, with the remaining 5840 tonnes still drying ahead of processing. The deal also provides a 12-month exclusive pathway for an additional 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes of yet-to-be-extracted transitional mixed ore (TMO) material from the broader Aktau stockpile, giving Lindian a clear sightline to a significantly bigger feedstock. In this specific operational setup, classification as TMO, rather than as a pure oxide or a primary ore, determines how the material must be prepared. Lindian Resources executive director Zac Komur said: “What makes this particularly interesting is the potential rare earth distribution. Kangankunde gives Lindian strong exposure to NdPr. Aktau provides us with the opportunity to establish whether we can add dysprosium, terbium and yttrium into the product suite through SARECO.” The strategic importance of this deal is layered. It gives Lindian the potential to produce a mixed heavy rare earth carbonate product, adding a high-value string to its bow and setting it apart from the neodymium-praseodymium concentrate planned to come from its flagship Kangankunde project. This also positions Lindian to tap into the critical dysprosium and terbium markets where supply outside of China is exceptionally tight, driving significant price premiums for non-China sourced material.

Advertisement

What makes this move even more strategically significant is the historical connection between the feedstock and the processing plant. The Aktau material was the original feedstock for the SARECO facility when it was commissioned in 2012, meaning the metallurgical and processing hard yards have already been addressed, substantially de-risking the venture. The already-established logistics have further bolstered Lindian’s planning. The Aktau-Stepnogorsk rail corridor was previously used to transport the same materials to the SARECO plant, giving Lindian a proven bulk transport solution. The arrangement offers Lindian immense operational flexibility. The Aktau material could be processed ahead of, alongside, or independently of concentrate deliveries from Kangankunde, which is targeting its first production in the fourth quarter of 2026. This timing could allow the SARECO facility to be commissioned and begin generating cash flow earlier than previously anticipated. Lindian is now undertaking sampling and metallurgical testwork to confirm the composition of the stockpiled material and its processing suitability, with initial results expected in the coming months. While the company notes no mineral resource has been defined for the stockpile, the historical links provide a solid foundation for its evaluation. Lindian’s acquisition of the SARECO plant in Kazakhstan always looked like a smart strategic play. Now, by potentially securing a historically proven, in-country feedstock for the plant, the company has added another layer of value to its downstream processing ambitions.

Advertisement

While all eyes have been on the development of its world-class Kangankunde mine in Malawi, Lindian’s Kazakh move shows the company is playing a multi-dimensional game by pursuing a two-pronged strategy, with a potential near-term, high-value heavy rare earths stream in Central Asia to complement its long-life, light rare earths production from Africa. title: Djokovic knocked out of US Open: Star loses in opening round of a major for first time in 20 years
text:

Breaking SportTennisUS Open Djokovic knocked out of US Open: Star loses in opening round of a major for first time in 20 years Marc McGowan Updated August 31, 2026 — 2:10pm ,first published August 31, 2026 — 8:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An ailing and tearful Novak Djokovic has suffered a shock first-round defeat at the US Open, losing at that stage of a grand slam for the first time in two decades. The 39-year-old grand slam legend showed signs of being physically compromised as early as the opening set – which he lost – but still managed to win the second and third sets, and was up a break in the fourth before everything changed. Novak Djokovic was in tears as his physical issues got the better of him in a first-round defeat. Getty Images Unheralded Argentinian Mariano Navone was responsible for Djokovic’s early exit, outlasting the 24-time major champion 7-6 (7-5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 across more than four-and-a-half hours on Arthur Ashe Stadium. Djokovic’s last first-round defeat at a grand slam was at the 2006 Australian Open. He said he considered retiring, but committed to playing on once he won the second and third sets.

Advertisement

Related Video Video icon 3:54 Tennis icon Djokovic reflects on 'difficult' relationship ”I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling on the court for me,” Djokovic said. “It’s something that I’ve been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year – vomiting, throwing up, a serious issue there, then my whole body starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain. The back just gave up in the end and [right] shoulder, and I couldn’t close it out. “I was a break up in the fourth, but just struggled all the way since the fourth game of the match. Again, I don’t want to take too much out of his win. Congrats to him. He’s a nice guy, a fighter, but I didn’t enjoy myself.” This tournament was viewed as a gilt-edged opportunity for him to claim an unprecedented 25th grand slam singles title without Jannik Sinner (knee) in the draw and Carlos Alcaraz (wrist) playing for the first time since April. But not even the great Novak Djokovic can deny Father Time.

Advertisement

He will drop outside the top 10 for the first time since mid-2018. Djokovic was violently ill at the back of the court after the sixth game of the third set and struggled with a lower back issue throughout the match, which he sought treatment for after losing the fourth set. Djokovic offered his appreciation to the New York crowd as he left the court. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II However, it was immediately obvious that the medical timeout between sets would not trigger a miraculous fightback when Djokovic sent down a first-serve fault at barely 162km/h, almost 30km/h slower than his typical delivery. He dropped serve minutes later to go 2-0 down and could never recover, cutting a forlorn and anguished figure as Navone’s inevitable victory excruciatingly played out. At one stage, Djokovic lost 18 of 21 points overlapping the fourth and fifth sets as he grimaced each time he moved.

Advertisement

Tears welled up in Djokovic’s eyes as his dramatic departure neared. By the end, he was rolling in serves and mostly attempting drop shots to keep points short while clearly being determined to complete the match. “It’s amazing the way we play. I mean, five sets against the GOAT [greatest of all-time] ... I’m very happy. I don’t know what I can say,” Navone said on court afterwards. “It’s unbelievable, and means a lot to me. I think it’s almost 12 o’clock [midnight, New York time], so we have to go to sleep.” Djokovic will have regrets that it came to this, given he also led Navone 3-0 and 4-1 in the opening set, on top of his 2-1 break advantage in the fourth. He has consistently stated he plans to continue his peerless career until the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. Australian wildcard Preston scores ‘special’ US Open win

Advertisement

Taylah Preston has capped her rapid rise to the world’s top 100 and ended Australia’s barren start to the US Open with a second grand slam match win this year. The 20-year-old wildcard backed up winning for the first time in a major at the Australian Open in January with a mature 6-3, 6-3 victory over big-hitting American Alycia Parks on Monday (AEST). Wildcard Taylah Preston advanced to the second round of the US Open with a win over local hope Alycia Parks. Getty Images “It’s really special,” said Preston, who was outside the top 200 in January. “I’m glad that my first grand slam win was in Australia, but hopefully, I can keep winning rounds at all the slams – not just at home.” There might be a dearth of men’s prospects in Australia beyond Cruz Hewitt, but Preston is part of a youth-led uprising on the women’s side, alongside Maya Joint, Talia Gibson and Emerson Jones.

Advertisement

Preston, who made her top-100 debut last week and is up to No.89 in the live rankings, was the sole victor on a challenging first day for Australians. Gibson, Adam Walton and Storm Hunter exited in the opening round, while two other Australians, Aleks Vukic and Kim Birrell, also face going out early. Loading Vukic trailed Japan’s former world junior No.1 Rei Sakamoto, 6-4, 6-7 (5-7), 6-4, 3-6, 4-3 (Sakamoto was 30-15 on serve), when rain caused officials to suspend play. Birrell is a set down and locked at three-all in the second-set tiebreaker with Croatia’s Petra Marcinko. Coached by Brett Hunter and Ash Barty’s former mentor Craig Tyzzer, Preston overcame deficits in each set to eliminate Parks in her second main draw appearance in New York. The West Australian wriggled out of a 0-40 hole in the third game before riding a break in the fifth game to a one-set advantage over Parks, whose waywardness contrasted greatly with Preston’s composed play.

Advertisement

However, an aggressive crosscourt backhand secured Parks an instant break in the second set as she tried to lift in front of her home fans. Parks had a game point on serve for a 3-0 lead, but repeatedly was her own worst enemy, whether double-faulting, spraying shots wide or long, or fluffing straightforward volleys. It was the latter that saw Parks gift Preston the break back in the second set. Talia Gibson fell narrowly short in her US Open first-round clash with Donna Vekic. Getty Images Preston had to dig deep after double-faulting to slip to 15-30 at two-all, but her emotions never wavered. Parks called for the trainer to have the strapping on her right shoulder readjusted, but it did not help her cause. Another double fault from the American on break point in the next game put Preston on the brink of victory – and the world No.100 completed the job.

Advertisement

Preston hit only eight winners compared to Parks’ 22, but committed 20 fewer unforced errors. Earlier, Gibson threatened to cause an upset before losing 6-2, 4-6, 6-3 to Croatian Donna Vekic. Loading Gibson, 22, has experienced a breakout year, earning a Billie Jean King Cup call-up and storming into the top 100 for the first time after a blistering few weeks at the Indian Wells and Miami Masters events, where she eliminated five top-20 stars. She even briefly became Australia’s top-ranked woman, but found herself a set and 4-1 down to Vekic – by a double-break deficit – in an error-strewn start before staging a mid-match revival.

Advertisement

Related Article US Open As the US Open begins, all eyes are on the big problem hurting tennis Vekic’s serving woes helped open the door as Gibson claimed 10 points in a row to grab one of the breaks back, hold serve, then reduce the former top-20 star to 0-30 in the eighth game, which turned into an enthralling back and forth. Eventually, an increasingly agitated Vekic wilted, delivering her sixth double fault overall and fourth in the second set to leave the set tied at four-all. Another Vekic double fault two games later sent the match to a decider. Everything seemed to be going Gibson’s way when she escaped from 0-40 in the opening game of the final set with some excellent first serves and a wonderfully struck forehand winner from deep in the court. Her big opportunity came in the ensuing minutes.

Advertisement

Vekic began spraying even the easiest of shots, offering two break points to Gibson that could have split open the match. Instead, Gibson let her off the hook with some loose errors, which became an unfortunate theme. Vekic finally made it out of the game on a mishit backhand that snuck inside the sideline and evaded Gibson’s racquet. Storm Hunter qualified for the draw, but was no match for Marta Kostyuk. Getty Images The stroke of fortune emboldened the Croatian, who secured the break on her third chance in Gibson’s next service game, which lasted more than 10 minutes and involved five deuces. Gibson brought up two consecutive break points to get back to three-all, only to again bail Vekic out as her last opportunities came and went.

Advertisement

Related Article US Open Demon’s tough draw and Tiley’s $150 million US Open splash “It’s a hard one to swallow,” Gibson said. “Most of the time it’s who makes the most unforced errors on the court who comes away with the loss, and today that was me, so it’s just something to learn from.” Hunter qualified for a grand slam main draw for the sixth time in her career, but was no match for Roland-Garros and Wimbledon semi-finalist Marta Kostyuk, the No.11 seed. Kostyuk breezed past Hunter 6-4, 6-1, while China’s Wu Yibing thumped 43 winners in downing Walton 7-6 (7-2), 6-2, 7-5.

Advertisement

Among the players to advance were 2024 runner-up Jessica Pegula, 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev and fellow seeds Elina Svitolina, Tommy Paul, Jasmine Paolini, Jiri Lehecka, Leylah Fernandez, Arthur Rinderknech, Ekaterina Alexandrova and Tomas Martin Etcheverry. However, dual grand slam winner Barbora Krejcikova lost 7-6 (7-4), 6-2 to Uzbekistan’s Kamilla Rakhimova, and British 29th seed Cam Norrie bowed out 6-7 (6-8), 6-2, 6-2, 6-3 to French up-and-comer Luca Van Assche. with AAP News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. title: Should smart glasses blur your face by default? Australia's watchdog thinks so
text:
In brief The Australian eSafety Commissioner has recommended changes to how smart glasses operate.

Further new protections will overhaul Australia's privacy laws related to social media, AI and smart glasses.

People's faces should automatically be blurred when being filmed by smart glasses as part of greater privacy measures, the online safety watchdog has urged.

In advice to industry, the eSafety Commissioner has called for extra protections to be put in place for smart glasses, or glasses with cameras attached to them.

The growing uptake of the technology, prompted by cheap versions of the products being sold in outlets such as Kmart, has increased concerns about privacy and people being filmed without their consent.

The commissioner said faces of people being filmed should be blurred by default if they have not given consent, with clearer indicators being given for when the glasses are recording video.

"Companies selling smart glasses must balance the benefits of the technology with the need to protect users and the public," the commissioner said.

"As smart glasses become more common, they may create new ways to perpetrate harms."

The eSafety Commissioner said the rapid evolution of the technology meant there was still a chance for extra safety features to be baked into the products before harms became more widespread.

"They may become increasingly interconnected with and create new ways to perpetrate different types of harms, such as image-based abuse, adult cyber abuse, cyberbullying of children, or the livestreaming of violent or other harmful content," the advice said.

"The harms linked to covert recording are not hypothetical. They are real and already occurring."

Among the concerns listed by the commissioner was how the glasses could be used by "pick-up artists" who use the glasses to film women without their knowledge.

"Most of the women do not realise they are being filmed. These posts often attract misogynistic comments, compounding the harm," the commissioner said.

"Used in this way, smart glasses can reinforce and normalise watching, recording and controlling women in public without their knowledge."

The commissioner has also called for livestreaming from the glasses to operate on a delay, as well as for recording to be disabled when the glasses are not being worn.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland wrote to the privacy commission earlier this month to investigate whether extra regulations for smart glasses were needed.

The Greens have called for a 12 month ban on the importation of smart glasses.

Under changes the minor party will bring to parliament, the filming, storing or sharing of footage from the glasses without consent would be a breach of privacy laws.

Social media and deletion requests

Rowland is also set to outline further changes to privacy laws, including the right to erasure, on Monday.

The policy would mean social media users can ask tech companies to delete their personal information published online or held by the platforms.

The draft laws will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles.

Rowland said the privacy laws were needed to keep up with technology changes.

"The right to erasure will help put more control in the hands of Australians, allowing personal information to be destroyed from large digital platforms," she said.

"We must ensure appropriate safeguards are placed around technology and stop the erosion of our privacy protections."

The federal government will also roll out extra protections for identity documents online.

A service called IDLock will allow people to block or unblock the use of identity documents such as passports.

IDLock will be made available through the government's MyGov platform from 2027 after a small-scale trial in late 2026.

"Australians deserve to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online," Rowland said.

"As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia's approach must evolve with them."

In brief Australian boxing legend Tony Mundine has died aged 75.

Mundine presided over a three-generation boxing dynasty including son Anthony and grandson Rahim.

Indigenous Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, aged 75.

The father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine succumbed to a heart attack on Sunday.

title: 'Massive changes': What you might find missing in Aussie supermarkets
text:
In Brief A social media trend known as "sardinemaxxing" has seen sardines cleared from supermarket shelves after hot demand.

Experts say the social media trend could be dangerous for other fish.

Walk down the canned fish aisle at your local supermarket right now, and there's a good chance you'll find a gap where the tinned sardines used to be, as a viral TikTok trend sends a wave of new fans in search of the small, oily fish.

The trend, dubbed "sardinemaxxing", has seen influencers push sardines as a beauty and wellness must-have, with some calling them "Botox on a fork" for their purported skin, hair, and anti-ageing benefits.

But experts say the trend raises real questions about where those sardines are coming from — and what happens if the hype spreads to other seafood.

Why groceries are going viral

Sardines are just the latest grocery item swept up in a social media-driven buying frenzy.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Cottage cheese and Greek yoghurt both had their moment in the past year, part of a broader "proteinmaxxing" wave prizing high-protein foods.

Lisa Asher, a retail and supermarket expert at the University of Sydney Business School, said the pattern is driven by a mix of influencer culture and wellness trends.

"What bothers me isn't that the kids are eating sardines … it's that they're taking advice now from people who are probably not people you should be listening to," Asher said.

"It's a new form of advertising with a lot of unknowns — we don't really know who's paying who and how much they're making out of it. That is a problem.

"In magazines, we used to look at celebrities, but celebrities have been replaced by influencers."

She said the trends all follow a similar pattern: demand increases, the product goes out of stock, prices sometimes rise, and eventually, when the hype cools down, it comes back in stock.

"But this is a product that is made from fish in the sea," she adds. "We don't want to overfish because suddenly, then we have none."

Canned sardines can be hard to come by these days thanks to a new social media trend. Source: Getty / Newscast / Universal Images Group

The big catch

That's where the environmental risks come in.

Adrian Meder, sustainable seafood program manager at the Australian Marine Conservation Society, says history shows a sudden cultural appetite for a particular seafood can do serious damage — pointing to shark fin soup, sea cucumber and some tuna fisheries as species pushed towards collapse by surging demand.

"We've yet to see online popularity as a driver of major declines in our oceans, but a cultural surge in popularity of a seafood has time and time again decimated populations of species from tunas, to sharks, to abalone, to sea cucumbers," Meder told SBS News.

"Online popularity is clearly capable of producing massive changes in consumer demand."

There's also a traceability problem: much of the tinned sardines on Australian shelves is imported, and it can be difficult to know where a can came from or how sustainably it was caught.

Jonathan Smart, an affiliate senior research scientist at James Cook University, agrees that origin matters.

He co-authored a study, released last week, that found Australia ranked just 52nd in seafood production, despite having about eight million square kilometres of fishing waters.

"The fisheries that a lot of our imported seafood comes from are actually quite unsustainable — and Australia imports a lot of seafood when perhaps it shouldn't," Smart told SBS News.

"By importing so much seafood, we're essentially exporting our environmental footprint to other countries that don't have the same level of management that we do."

He worries a viral trend like this one could make that problem worse.

"If a trend like this is popping up and all of a sudden you've got greater consumption of a species, the fear I would have is that then is going to lead to, again, a greater surge in that imported seafood.

"We just don't know if that's going to have the same sustainability levels as if you were actually consuming something locally."

A resilient little fish

But of all the species to go viral, sardines might be one of the best placed to handle their 15 minutes of fame.

Smart says sardines are a fast-growing, short-lived species with rapid turnover, making them naturally resilient to heavy fishing.

Because changes in biomass are driven more by environmental conditions — like ocean upwellings — rather than fishing activity, sardine and anchovy fisheries are some of the biggest in the world, he said.

"They can actually provide a really, really big harvest from them normally under sustainable conditions, depending on the fishery that they're coming from."

Locally, there's also a genuine opportunity: Australia's biggest fishery is a sardine fishery in South Australia — a fact Smart says is little known because much of the catch goes to aquaculture feed.

"Very little of it actually goes to human consumption," he said. "That's why I often recommend to people that we should be eating more sardines because that is a really sustainable fishery.

"We catch a lot of fish from it, and there's a lot of opportunity."

Meder agrees that there's room for Australians to put more sardines on their plate.

"Some cultures, including many Australian communities, actually used to eat a lot more sardines than they do now," he said, pointing to a shift in seafood consumption to more environmentally vulnerable, less abundant, and expensive fish species — of which trends like these could help reverse.

But that only holds if the sardines on the shelf are actually Australian — which means consumers may need to check labels and do a bit of Googling before putting them in their shopping basket.

So while sardines may be getting the limelight for just a brief period before scrollers move on to the next trend, if there's anything we can take from it, it's that the humble little sardine is actually built for this moment.

title: What we know as Australia's bird flu outbreak enters a grim new chapter
text:
In brief A seal, a dolphin and a fox have tested positive for H5 bird flu in South Australia.

Experts share advice on protecting pets and wildlife as the outbreak grows.

Bird flu has begun its spread beyond birds in Australia, with cases confirmed in three different mammal species since last weekend.

On Friday, Australia's chief veterinary officer, Beth Cookson, said H5 bird flu had been confirmed in a red fox found in metropolitan Adelaide, marking the first in a land mammal in Australia.

A dead dolphin found on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula also tested positive this week, days after a long-nosed fur seal found dead at Beachport became the country's first mainland mammal case.

How does bird flu spread in mammals?

Bird flu has been detected in many different mammals on other continents, including cats and dogs, farm animals, dolphins, seals, foxes, tigers, leopards and polar bears.

Infected birds spread the virus through droppings, feathers and other bodily fluids. It can also be transmitted via contaminated clothing, footwear, equipment and vehicles.

Under favourable conditions, the virus can survive in the environment for months, Australian government authorities have said.

While the virus primarily spreads from infected birds, there is evidence it can also spread between some mammals, including during outbreaks in seals and dairy cattle overseas.

READ MORE 'Contaminated': How deadly bird flu crossed a new threshold in Australia

Among scavengers like foxes and cats, infections have been linked to eating or interacting with bird carcasses.

Cookson said there was no evidence of mammal-to-mammal transmission of the virus in Australia.

"This detection in a fox is a good reminder that people and their pets should avoid sick or dead wildlife," Cookson said on Friday.

READ MORE Rush to vaccinate little penguins against H5N1 as another seal is diagnosed

"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected given that H5 bird flu has been detected in other wildlife in areas where there are high levels of infection in wild birds."

She said the risk to human health remains low.

Which Australian mammals are most at risk?

The government's H5 bird flu risk assessment ranks multiple dolphin, seal and sea lion species among Australia's most vulnerable native mammals, and experts fear the virus could have devastating consequences for endangered species such as the Australian sea lion.

Seal populations around the world have proved particularly vulnerable to bird flu outbreaks.

The virus decimated southern elephant seal populations on Heard Island after reaching the Australian sub-antarctic territory last year, killing an estimated 75 per cent of pups.

Jane Younger, senior lecturer in Southern Ocean vertebrate ecology at the University of Tasmania, said it was "devastating news for wildlife" that bird flu had been detected in a mainland Australian mammal.

"My biggest concern now is the endangered Australian sea lion, which is found nowhere else in the world," she said.

"Infected and dying seabirds have already been found at important sea lion breeding sites around Kangaroo Island. If the virus enters a breeding colony, there is no way to stop it spreading."

She called for intensive surveillance of seal and sea lion colonies, rapid genome sequencing of mammal cases and an urgent investigation of whether targeted vaccinations could help protect certain populations.

South Australian Environment Minister Emily Bourke said last week that her state would assess the possibility of importing an experimental US vaccine for use among mammals in Australia, but warned that vaccines for mammals such as cattle and cats being developed overseas are yet to be approved by authorities.

The use of vaccines in birds is further advanced, with Australian officials saying last year that a H5 vaccine had been procured and authorised for use in particular rare, protected or valuable bird populations.

Victoria is currently vaccinating thousands of little penguins, which are a popular tourist attraction.

Should we be worried about our cats and dogs?

Bird flu infections have been reported in domestic cats and dogs overseas, though the Australian government says such infections are uncommon and usually occur through contact with infected birds.

Symptoms may include fever, lethargy, decreased appetite, red or inflamed eyes, discharge from eyes and nose, coughing and sneezing, and tremors.

Cat owners should be particularly mindful, Robyn Alders, an animal influenza expert and honorary professor at the Australian National University's Crawford School of Public Health, told SBS News.

Overseas, cats infected with the virus have experienced a high mortality rate.

She suggests keeping cats indoors, especially in areas where bird flu cases have been confirmed, and keeping dogs on a leash when walking.

The virus can also be spread through contaminated food and water, so experts recommend keeping pets' bowls inside or out of reach of wild birds.

Australians visiting wetlands, beaches, farms or wildlife areas are advised to observe wildlife from a distance, avoid contact with sick or dead animals, and to clean footwear and equipment with detergent or disinfectant.

Alders suggests that pet owners who go for walks in areas where sick or dead animals have been found could consider keeping a separate pair of walking shoes that they always disinfect.

title: More Australians are buying homes later. What does that mean for retirement?
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Damian Hole's last mortgage repayment is due when he's 80.

The 52-year-old bought his first home about a decade ago and refinanced it in 2024, locking in a new 30-year loan term just before he turned 50.

He's among a growing cohort of Australians buying their first home later in life. People over the age of 40 accounted for nearly one in five first-home buyers last year (18.7 per cent), according to data from one of Australia's largest mortgage brokers, Aussie Home Loans.

That's up from just over 5.5 per cent in 2005.

At the other end, people under the age of 20 made up around a quarter of first-home buyers in 2005, compared with less than 0.5 per cent in 2025.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

As housing affordability pressures make it harder for young Australians to enter the market, solutions designed to ease the path to home ownership have increasingly focused on expanding access to credit — allowing buyers to borrow more, with smaller deposits or longer mortgage terms.

Low-deposit loans can be accessed through the federal government's 5 per cent deposit scheme, while family guarantor loans allow first-time buyers to borrow up to 100 per cent of the purchase price.

A growing cohort of Australians are buying their first home later in life. Source: SBS News

Meanwhile, more lenders are offering 40-year mortgage terms, meaning some borrowers could be signing up to make repayments well into their later years.

If a growing number of Australians are buying homes later while taking on larger loans for longer, what happens when they reach retirement still saddled with mortgage debt?

'A cat and mouse game'

Making it easier for people to borrow can fuel higher house prices.

According to James Graham, a housing economics expert at the University of Sydney, without massively expanding housing supply, broadening access to credit alone is not a sustainable solution.

"It's just sort of a cat-and-mouse game," Graham tells SBS News.

"The prices go up, so we change mortgage credit. That pushes prices up further.

People are just borrowing more to buy more expensive houses, and they're not really any better off.

When the government introduced its 5 per cent deposit scheme last year, designed to help first-home buyers, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) predicted the measure would likely "put at least some further upward pressure" on housing price growth.

By March, the value of new loans taken out by first-home buyers was around 11 per cent higher than before the scheme was expanded in October, with the increase largely reflecting bigger average loan sizes, according to the RBA.

The costs of delayed home ownership

Graham says buying a first home later in life could have consequences beyond carrying mortgage debt into retirement. Entering the market at 40 or 50 leaves less time to build housing wealth and can reduce people's ability to move as their lives change.

"People are likely to be locked in for longer," he explains, warning that some buyers may end up remaining in homes that were intended as a first step into the market rather than a last stop.

"Less moving has its own social consequences," he adds.

"It means that people can't move back to communities that they wanted to be part of; they're further away from their children than they wanted to be; they're not near jobs that they want to be near.

"Maybe they've moved far out of the city because that's the only place they could buy. But now they're away from amenities and doctors."

Delayed home ownership and larger mortgages could also have implications for the aged care sector. Traditionally, many older Australians have relied on accessing housing equity (the portion of a property that is owned outright) to help fund retirement living or aged care, often through selling the family home. Unsettled mortgage debt could affect this transition, reducing the overall equity available.

Another concern is long-term mortgage stress, which can reduce the wellbeing of older Australians and may lead retirees to draw down their superannuation to pay off housing debt, according to 2019 research from the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI).

This, in turn, could place additional pressure on the pension system.

Currently, the Age Pension excludes the primary home from its assets test.

Paying down mortgage debt on a primary home with super can, therefore, reduce a person's assessable assets and potentially make them eligible for the pension.

"We have an ageing population in Australia, so the fiscal pressure on government will increase with that if government is supporting people through the pension system," AHURI managing director Tom Alves tells SBS News.

"The compulsory superannuation system is designed to address that issue, and if people are not having enough income through their super because they've used it to pay off their mortgage, obviously that's an issue."

AHURI's research notes that mortgage debt was uncommon among people aged 55-64 as early as the 1990s. Between 1996 and 2013, however, the proportion of Australians in that age bracket still paying off a mortgage rose from under 20 per cent to 45 per cent.

Home ownership has long underpinned Australia's retirement system, with policies, including the Age Pension, built on the assumption that most retirees own their home.

Widely used superannuation savings targets typically assume that people will own their homes outright by the time they reach retirement. While some modelling also considers renters, retirees still paying off a mortgage are largely left out of the picture.

"They do assume that people own their home," Susan Thorp, a retirement finance specialist at Monash University, tells SBS News.

"They're not allowing for the idea that someone may have, say, $150,000 of mortgage debt at the time they're retiring."

Yet a growing share of Australians may not fit those assumptions. In a January survey of 1,020 people by Loan Market Group, 58 per cent said they planned to own their home before retirement.

The rise of the 40-year mortgage

A small but growing number of Australian lenders have started offering 40-year mortgage terms, which can give borrowers access to loans they might not otherwise have been able to afford — but can add staggering extra interest costs over the life of the loan.

Source: SBS News

Richard Brown, a Mortgage Choice broker in the Sydney suburb of Epping, says many of his clients are eager to find ways to maximise their borrowing power, which is increasing their appetite for longer loan terms despite the downsides.

"There's an appetite for borrowers to get access to the money they need to buy the property they want," he says.

"They don't care what it is."

Sebastian Watkins, CEO and co-founder of mortgage broking giant Lendi Group, says relying on borrowing innovations like longer loan terms risks overlooking the underlying issue of unaffordable housing prices.

"We can't simply respond to people taking longer to save by giving them longer to pay off their loan," he tells SBS News.

If current trends continue, in a decade or two, Watkins expects the average Australian mortgage to be "larger, held later in life and managed much more dynamically".

We are likely to see longer loan terms, more family-supported or multi-generational borrowing and products that adapt as a customer's income, family circumstances and property needs change.

Japan offers an extreme historical example of intergenerational borrowing. Amid soaring housing costs in the 1980s, it experimented with 100-year mortgages designed to be repaid across multiple generations. Researchers who later modelled the loans concluded they did little to improve housing affordability.

What happens when debt stretches beyond careers?

Lenders assessing older applicants will typically look for a credible exit strategy demonstrating the loan can be comfortably managed in retirement, Watkins says.

"They may look at the expected loan balance at retirement age and consider the borrower's projected superannuation and other assets. Another potential strategy could be downsizing, where the borrower could sell the property and purchase a lower-value home," he says.

Hole, who bought his first home at 42, says his bank requested his superannuation balance before approving his mortgage.

"It was almost done, and then they requested my super balance, and then I realised, because my age will go beyond retirement, they're just seeing if I've got enough super to pay off the loan."

He says he should be able to comfortably repay the remainder of his mortgage with a lump sum from his super when he reaches retirement age, at which point he intends to access the Age Pension.

Damian Hole, 52, lives in Bacchus Marsh, Victoria, with his wife and three kids. Source: Supplied

The retirement debt challenge

Alves says there is no single policy fix, but governments need to consider both retirement and housing policy together.

Potential approaches include adjusting Age Pension settings to better reflect the differences between homeowners and non-homeowners, as well as expanding affordable housing options for older Australians, he says.

More broadly, he says improving access to home ownership earlier in life and increasing the supply of affordable rental housing could help reduce the number of Australians entering retirement with housing stress.

Thorp says there are fundamental questions that remain unanswered about what happens when more Australians enter retirement with housing debt.

"The question of how housing policy merges with superannuation and retirement policy is not fully worked out," she says.

title: Australian woman feared missing in Nepal flood makes contact as disaster worsens
text:
Australian authorities are urgently trying to reach a woman who made contact with family after surviving catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-China border.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) is engaging with local authorities on plans to assist the woman, who is understood to have been last reported in a remote area several days' hike from Kathmandu.

At least 38 Australians remain missing after an ice avalanche on Wednesday triggered Nepal's worst natural disaster in more than a decade.

Heavy continued rainfall is making rescue conditions difficult and unpredictable.

Further severe flooding, landslides and debris flows are predicted in the affected areas of Nepal and Tibet while a lake formed by the landslide has started to overflow.

At least 538 people have died, Nepalese authorities said, while almost 1,000 remain missing.

Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was on a pilgrimage on the China-Nepal border when the catastrophic flash flooding hit.

Her husband Kailash Mansowar, who has not heard from her since, has travelled to the region from Sydney to find her, guided only by her iPhone's last location.

"I am here in Nepal now (since) yesterday and working with local authorities to find further information," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) on Friday.

Like many missing Australians, Adhikari was undertaking a group tour, in her case with the Isha Foundation.

She left Kathmandu on 14 August after flying from Sydney to trek to a sacred site near Tibet's Mount Kailash.

"Even the smallest piece of information could help bring her home," a widely shared post on social media announcing her disappearance reads.

A separate group of 15 Australians, including two boys aged 11 and 14, were travelling with US-based tourism operator Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company.

Sydney doctor Manoj Dharmaratnam, who was invited to join the sacred pilgrimage but chose not to go, prescribed several of his friends altitude medication and conducted injury assessments before they left Australia.

"One of them had an injury and I did tell her, maybe you're not fit to go on this trek," Dr Dharmaratnam told AAP.

"She actually called up and cancelled her trip ... but then she said I've bought the ticket, so I might as well go."

The Himalayan Glacier group included a well-respected Sydney couple with two sons in their 20s, both studying medicine in NSW, he said.

READ MORE How Australians can help those impacted by devastating Nepal floods

At least four Australians were travelling separately to tour groups, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Friday.

Wong said the federal government would send additional personnel to the region and unveiled a $5 million assistance package and humanitarian support.

An initial team of three humanitarian response specialists will be sent to help 20 staff already on the ground in Nepal.

But Chinese and Nepalese authorities say local rescue efforts could be complicated by further flooding, caused by a build-up of debris.

READ MORE Nepal's glacier collapse sends a warning beyond the Himalayas

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Thursday warned a lake was forming above the Rasuwagadhi border.

By Friday it had begun to overflow.

The Lhendi River had been obstructed about 18 kilometres above the border, posing a risk to residents in areas below, it said in a statement on social media.

The threat of a second flood caused by a blockage upstream led to evacuation orders at Jilong Port on the Nepal-China border, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

Rocks, boulders and debris lodged in the valley, as well as lakes forming along the plateau, could cause further flooding, geoscientist Jakob Steiner told AAP.

"Unfortunately it's not over ... this material is only going to lie there. We cannot move it away," Steiner, a fellow at the Asian Mountain Alliance, said.

"Every time a new flood comes, it's going to move this, and this is just going to increase future flood events in terms of impact."

title: How Australians can help those impacted by devastating Nepal floods
text:
IN BRIEF Donations will help provide emergency shelter, food, clean water, hygiene supplies and medical care.

Australians can donate through the Emergency Action Alliance's Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal or by calling 1300 939 000.

Entire communities have been devastated by severe flooding and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border, with homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure destroyed.

Search and rescue operations remain underway, while thousands of people are in urgent need of shelter, food, clean drinking water and medical assistance.

In response, 14 Australian charities have joined forces to launch a national appeal.

Emergency Action Alliance

The Emergency Action Alliance (EAA) has launched the Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal, bringing together a variety of charities to support communities affected by the disaster.

The alliance says donations will help provide immediate humanitarian assistance, including emergency shelter, food, safe drinking water, hygiene supplies and medical care.

Access to some affected communities remains difficult, with damaged roads and ongoing weather conditions hampering efforts to reach people in need.

Australians are encouraged to donate through the EAA website or by calling 1300 939 000.

READ MORE Nepal army races to save 100 people trapped in tunnel as flood death toll rises over 530

The charities participating in the appeal are Save the Children Australia, Plan International Australia, Oxfam Australia, Australia for UNHCR, ActionAid Australia, CARE Australia, Caritas Australia, ADRA, Act for Peace, Anglican Overseas Aid, Australian Lutheran World Service, Baptist World Aid Australia, CBM Australia and Tearfund Australia.

EAA executive director Kerren Morris said the appeal provided Australians with a trusted way to support people affected by the disaster.

"Emergency shelter, food, safe drinking water and medical support are urgently needed now, while longer-term recovery efforts will continue for many months," she said in a statement.

What are the charities doing?

The charities involved bring different areas of humanitarian expertise to the response, with organisations and their local partners working to provide immediate assistance to affected communities.

Save the Children Australia

Save the Children is focusing on supporting children and families affected by humanitarian emergencies.

Oxfam Australia

Oxfam Australia's humanitarian work includes support for essential services such as clean water, sanitation and emergency assistance.

Australia for UNHCR

Australia for UNHCR is the UN refugee agency's national partner in Australia, and is supporting humanitarian assistance through the UNHCR network.

Homes and buildings have been left damaged and filled with debris after devastating flash floods swept through communities in Nepal. Source: Getty / Anadolu / Sunil Pradhan

What happens to donations?

The charities involved are continuing to assess the scale of the disaster and humanitarian needs in affected communities.

The EAA says its members are working to determine where support is most urgently needed as search and rescue operations continue.

The appeal has been endorsed by the Australian Council for International Development (ACFID), the peak body for Australian non-government organisations involved in humanitarian action and international development.

The ABC is also supporting the appeal through its ABC Gives initiative.

ACFID CEO Matthew Maury said coordinated action was critical as humanitarian needs continued to emerge.

"This appeal provides Australians with a trusted and effective way to support communities affected by this disaster," he said.

Australia pledges $5 million in aid

The Australian government has confirmed a $5 million humanitarian assistance package for communities affected by the devastating floods along the Nepal-China border.

The funding will support both the immediate disaster response and longer-term recovery, with the government saying it will help provide food, emergency shelter, clean water and sanitation.

READ MORE Nepal's glacier collapse sends a warning beyond the Himalayas

The $5 million package will be delivered through established humanitarian partners, including $2 million to the World Food Programme for food and logistical support, $2 million through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership for emergency assistance including shelter, hygiene kits, blankets, medical care and psychosocial support, and $1 million to the EAA to support locally led recovery and rehabilitation efforts.

Assistant Foreign Affairs Minister Matt Thistlethwaite said Australian officials were working with Nepali authorities and tour operators to understand the situation and assess the needs of those affected.

Thistlethwaite also said the government was "working around the clock" to verify the status of Australians in the region, but damaged roads and telecommunications infrastructure were making it difficult to establish contact.

More Australian support on the way

Australia will also deploy three humanitarian specialists to Nepal within 48 hours to help assess needs and support the emergency response.

The specialists are being deployed through the Australia Assists program and have expertise in humanitarian assessment, logistics, communications and planning.

A crisis response team member and a regional consular officer are already on the ground in Kathmandu, alongside staff at the Australian embassy.

Australians in the affected region

Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the scale of the disaster and the remoteness of the affected region meant there were "immense challenges" ahead for the response and recovery.

"With roads and bridges destroyed, many communities remain isolated and difficult to reach, underscoring the need for rapid humanitarian assistance," she said.

The government's humanitarian response comes as Australian officials continue to try to establish the whereabouts of Australians caught up in the disaster.

The latest government figure is at least 39 Australians reported missing.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is working with Nepali authorities, tour operators and others to verify their welfare and contact their families.

Australians requiring emergency consular assistance can contact the 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135 in Australia or +61 2 6261 3305 from overseas.

The government is also urging Australians in affected areas to follow the advice of local authorities and monitor official travel advice.

title: Lindian locks in early feed for Kazakh heavy rare earths plant
text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Lindian locks in early feed for Kazakh heavy rare earths plant Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright August 31, 2026 — 2:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In a savvy strategic move, Lindian Resources has executed an exclusive option to secure a substantial heavy rare earth minerals stockpile in Kazakhstan. The material could become a ready-made feed source for its recently acquired Summit Atom Rare Earth Company’s (SARECO) hydrometallurgical processing facility in the central Asian nation. The deal gives Lindian the right to acquire an initial 13,389 tonnes of previously extracted material from the Aktau stockpile, which contains the sought-after heavy rare earth elements dysprosium, terbium and yttrium. Lindian Resources’ recently acquired processing infrastructure within the SARECO mixed rare earths carbonate (MREC) facility. The move is a notable coup for Lindian and complements its massive Kangankunde light rare earth minerals project in Malawi, East Africa. It potentially fast-tracks the company’s entry into the lucrative heavy “magnet” rare earths market, which supplies the vital ingredients of high-powered magnets used in the construction of electric vehicles, power generation equipment and a growing range of advanced medical, electronic and defence technologies. SARECO was initially established as a high-level, multinational joint venture between two institutional giants, Kazatomprom and Sumitomo Corporation, to recover rare earth elements from uranium-derived residues, commissioning the Stepnogorsk facility in 2012. Ore material from Aktau was supplied to SARECO, making it directly relevant to Lindian’s evaluation of the opportunity today.

Advertisement

‘Aktau is strategically important because it was historically used as feedstock for SARECO.’ Lindian Resources executive director Zac Komur Years after commissioning, the original Kazatomprom-Sumitomo partnership dissolved due to severe feedstock constraints and a shift in corporate strategy. When the facility went dormant, the original founders ultimately sold the asset and transferred it out of their portfolios. Kazakhstan-based RA-Group LLP acquired the idle facility following the original founders’ exit. Rather than being a pioneer miner from 2012, RA Group acted as the local Kazakhstan entity which consolidated the asset’s land, warehouses and infrastructure. Lindian originally announced a joint venture framework with RA-Group in March 2026, under which it would acquire a 51% majority interest in the SARECO processing facility for an initial valuation. When the deal was first struck, RA-Group held the remaining 49% interest in the incorporated joint venture alongside Lindian’s 51 per cent. Following extensive due diligence, Lindian shifted strategy to secure 100 per cent ownership of the SARECO facility in early August, a move which strongly reflected the broader opportunity Lindian had identified at SARECO. RA-Group LLP negotiated a substantial exit package, becoming the direct recipient of up to US$22 million (A$30.72M) in Lindian equity, comprising US$15 million (A$20.94M) in fully paid ordinary shares and US$7 million (A$9.77M) in milestone-driven performance rights.

Advertisement

Under the terms of its latest agreement with SARECO, Lindian has nailed down the option over the initial stockpile, with no upfront cash consideration payable. The company says 7549 tonnes of the material have already been identified as ready for transport, with the remaining 5840 tonnes still drying ahead of processing. The deal also provides a 12-month exclusive pathway for an additional 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes of yet-to-be-extracted transitional mixed ore (TMO) material from the broader Aktau stockpile, giving Lindian a clear sightline to a significantly bigger feedstock. In this specific operational setup, classification as TMO, rather than as a pure oxide or a primary ore, determines how the material must be prepared. Lindian Resources executive director Zac Komur said: “What makes this particularly interesting is the potential rare earth distribution. Kangankunde gives Lindian strong exposure to NdPr. Aktau provides us with the opportunity to establish whether we can add dysprosium, terbium and yttrium into the product suite through SARECO.” The strategic importance of this deal is layered. It gives Lindian the potential to produce a mixed heavy rare earth carbonate product, adding a high-value string to its bow and setting it apart from the neodymium-praseodymium concentrate planned to come from its flagship Kangankunde project. This also positions Lindian to tap into the critical dysprosium and terbium markets where supply outside of China is exceptionally tight, driving significant price premiums for non-China sourced material.

Advertisement

What makes this move even more strategically significant is the historical connection between the feedstock and the processing plant. The Aktau material was the original feedstock for the SARECO facility when it was commissioned in 2012, meaning the metallurgical and processing hard yards have already been addressed, substantially de-risking the venture. The already-established logistics have further bolstered Lindian’s planning. The Aktau-Stepnogorsk rail corridor was previously used to transport the same materials to the SARECO plant, giving Lindian a proven bulk transport solution. The arrangement offers Lindian immense operational flexibility. The Aktau material could be processed ahead of, alongside, or independently of concentrate deliveries from Kangankunde, which is targeting its first production in the fourth quarter of 2026. This timing could allow the SARECO facility to be commissioned and begin generating cash flow earlier than previously anticipated. Lindian is now undertaking sampling and metallurgical testwork to confirm the composition of the stockpiled material and its processing suitability, with initial results expected in the coming months. While the company notes no mineral resource has been defined for the stockpile, the historical links provide a solid foundation for its evaluation. Lindian’s acquisition of the SARECO plant in Kazakhstan always looked like a smart strategic play. Now, by potentially securing a historically proven, in-country feedstock for the plant, the company has added another layer of value to its downstream processing ambitions.

While all eyes have been on the development of its world-class Kangankunde mine in Malawi, Lindian’s Kazakh move shows the company is playing a multi-dimensional game by pursuing a two-pronged strategy, with a potential near-term, high-value heavy rare earths stream in Central Asia to complement its long-life, light rare earths production from Africa. title: Djokovic knocked out of US Open: Star loses in opening round of a major for first time in 20 years
text:
Advertisement

Breaking SportTennisUS Open Djokovic knocked out of US Open: Star loses in opening round of a major for first time in 20 years Marc McGowan Updated August 31, 2026 — 2:10pm ,first published August 31, 2026 — 8:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An ailing and tearful Novak Djokovic has suffered a shock first-round defeat at the US Open, losing at that stage of a grand slam for the first time in two decades. The 39-year-old grand slam legend showed signs of being physically compromised as early as the opening set – which he lost – but still managed to win the second and third sets, and was up a break in the fourth before everything changed. Novak Djokovic was in tears as his physical issues got the better of him in a first-round defeat. Getty Images Unheralded Argentinian Mariano Navone was responsible for Djokovic’s early exit, outlasting the 24-time major champion 7-6 (7-5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 across more than four-and-a-half hours on Arthur Ashe Stadium. Djokovic’s last first-round defeat at a grand slam was at the 2006 Australian Open. He said he considered retiring, but committed to playing on once he won the second and third sets.

Advertisement

Related Video Video icon 3:54 Tennis icon Djokovic reflects on 'difficult' relationship ”I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling on the court for me,” Djokovic said. “It’s something that I’ve been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year – vomiting, throwing up, a serious issue there, then my whole body starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain. The back just gave up in the end and [right] shoulder, and I couldn’t close it out. “I was a break up in the fourth, but just struggled all the way since the fourth game of the match. Again, I don’t want to take too much out of his win. Congrats to him. He’s a nice guy, a fighter, but I didn’t enjoy myself.” This tournament was viewed as a gilt-edged opportunity for him to claim an unprecedented 25th grand slam singles title without Jannik Sinner (knee) in the draw and Carlos Alcaraz (wrist) playing for the first time since April. But not even the great Novak Djokovic can deny Father Time.

Advertisement

He will drop outside the top 10 for the first time since mid-2018. Djokovic was violently ill at the back of the court after the sixth game of the third set and struggled with a lower back issue throughout the match, which he sought treatment for after losing the fourth set. Djokovic offered his appreciation to the New York crowd as he left the court. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II However, it was immediately obvious that the medical timeout between sets would not trigger a miraculous fightback when Djokovic sent down a first-serve fault at barely 162km/h, almost 30km/h slower than his typical delivery. He dropped serve minutes later to go 2-0 down and could never recover, cutting a forlorn and anguished figure as Navone’s inevitable victory excruciatingly played out. At one stage, Djokovic lost 18 of 21 points overlapping the fourth and fifth sets as he grimaced each time he moved.

Advertisement

Tears welled up in Djokovic’s eyes as his dramatic departure neared. By the end, he was rolling in serves and mostly attempting drop shots to keep points short while clearly being determined to complete the match. “It’s amazing the way we play. I mean, five sets against the GOAT [greatest of all-time] ... I’m very happy. I don’t know what I can say,” Navone said on court afterwards. “It’s unbelievable, and means a lot to me. I think it’s almost 12 o’clock [midnight, New York time], so we have to go to sleep.” Djokovic will have regrets that it came to this, given he also led Navone 3-0 and 4-1 in the opening set, on top of his 2-1 break advantage in the fourth. He has consistently stated he plans to continue his peerless career until the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. Australian wildcard Preston scores ‘special’ US Open win

Advertisement

Taylah Preston has capped her rapid rise to the world’s top 100 and ended Australia’s barren start to the US Open with a second grand slam match win this year. The 20-year-old wildcard backed up winning for the first time in a major at the Australian Open in January with a mature 6-3, 6-3 victory over big-hitting American Alycia Parks on Monday (AEST). Wildcard Taylah Preston advanced to the second round of the US Open with a win over local hope Alycia Parks. Getty Images “It’s really special,” said Preston, who was outside the top 200 in January. “I’m glad that my first grand slam win was in Australia, but hopefully, I can keep winning rounds at all the slams – not just at home.” There might be a dearth of men’s prospects in Australia beyond Cruz Hewitt, but Preston is part of a youth-led uprising on the women’s side, alongside Maya Joint, Talia Gibson and Emerson Jones.

Advertisement

Preston, who made her top-100 debut last week and is up to No.89 in the live rankings, was the sole victor on a challenging first day for Australians. Gibson, Adam Walton and Storm Hunter exited in the opening round, while two other Australians, Aleks Vukic and Kim Birrell, also face going out early. Loading Vukic trailed Japan’s former world junior No.1 Rei Sakamoto, 6-4, 6-7 (5-7), 6-4, 3-6, 4-3 (Sakamoto was 30-15 on serve), when rain caused officials to suspend play. Birrell is a set down and locked at three-all in the second-set tiebreaker with Croatia’s Petra Marcinko. Coached by Brett Hunter and Ash Barty’s former mentor Craig Tyzzer, Preston overcame deficits in each set to eliminate Parks in her second main draw appearance in New York. The West Australian wriggled out of a 0-40 hole in the third game before riding a break in the fifth game to a one-set advantage over Parks, whose waywardness contrasted greatly with Preston’s composed play.

Advertisement

However, an aggressive crosscourt backhand secured Parks an instant break in the second set as she tried to lift in front of her home fans. Parks had a game point on serve for a 3-0 lead, but repeatedly was her own worst enemy, whether double-faulting, spraying shots wide or long, or fluffing straightforward volleys. It was the latter that saw Parks gift Preston the break back in the second set. Talia Gibson fell narrowly short in her US Open first-round clash with Donna Vekic. Getty Images Preston had to dig deep after double-faulting to slip to 15-30 at two-all, but her emotions never wavered. Parks called for the trainer to have the strapping on her right shoulder readjusted, but it did not help her cause. Another double fault from the American on break point in the next game put Preston on the brink of victory – and the world No.100 completed the job.

Advertisement

Preston hit only eight winners compared to Parks’ 22, but committed 20 fewer unforced errors. Earlier, Gibson threatened to cause an upset before losing 6-2, 4-6, 6-3 to Croatian Donna Vekic. Loading Gibson, 22, has experienced a breakout year, earning a Billie Jean King Cup call-up and storming into the top 100 for the first time after a blistering few weeks at the Indian Wells and Miami Masters events, where she eliminated five top-20 stars. She even briefly became Australia’s top-ranked woman, but found herself a set and 4-1 down to Vekic – by a double-break deficit – in an error-strewn start before staging a mid-match revival.

Advertisement

Related Article US Open As the US Open begins, all eyes are on the big problem hurting tennis Vekic’s serving woes helped open the door as Gibson claimed 10 points in a row to grab one of the breaks back, hold serve, then reduce the former top-20 star to 0-30 in the eighth game, which turned into an enthralling back and forth. Eventually, an increasingly agitated Vekic wilted, delivering her sixth double fault overall and fourth in the second set to leave the set tied at four-all. Another Vekic double fault two games later sent the match to a decider. Everything seemed to be going Gibson’s way when she escaped from 0-40 in the opening game of the final set with some excellent first serves and a wonderfully struck forehand winner from deep in the court. Her big opportunity came in the ensuing minutes.

Advertisement

Vekic began spraying even the easiest of shots, offering two break points to Gibson that could have split open the match. Instead, Gibson let her off the hook with some loose errors, which became an unfortunate theme. Vekic finally made it out of the game on a mishit backhand that snuck inside the sideline and evaded Gibson’s racquet. Storm Hunter qualified for the draw, but was no match for Marta Kostyuk. Getty Images The stroke of fortune emboldened the Croatian, who secured the break on her third chance in Gibson’s next service game, which lasted more than 10 minutes and involved five deuces. Gibson brought up two consecutive break points to get back to three-all, only to again bail Vekic out as her last opportunities came and went.

Advertisement

Related Article US Open Demon’s tough draw and Tiley’s $150 million US Open splash “It’s a hard one to swallow,” Gibson said. “Most of the time it’s who makes the most unforced errors on the court who comes away with the loss, and today that was me, so it’s just something to learn from.” Hunter qualified for a grand slam main draw for the sixth time in her career, but was no match for Roland-Garros and Wimbledon semi-finalist Marta Kostyuk, the No.11 seed. Kostyuk breezed past Hunter 6-4, 6-1, while China’s Wu Yibing thumped 43 winners in downing Walton 7-6 (7-2), 6-2, 7-5.

Advertisement

Among the players to advance were 2024 runner-up Jessica Pegula, 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev and fellow seeds Elina Svitolina, Tommy Paul, Jasmine Paolini, Jiri Lehecka, Leylah Fernandez, Arthur Rinderknech, Ekaterina Alexandrova and Tomas Martin Etcheverry. However, dual grand slam winner Barbora Krejcikova lost 7-6 (7-4), 6-2 to Uzbekistan’s Kamilla Rakhimova, and British 29th seed Cam Norrie bowed out 6-7 (6-8), 6-2, 6-2, 6-3 to French up-and-comer Luca Van Assche. with AAP News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Barkly NT test cracks 99% magnet rare earths extraction Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 31, 2026 — 1:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

ASX-listed Barkly Rare Earths has announced a stunning 99 per cent extraction of high-value magnet rare earth oxides (MREO) from a single-stage metallurgical test on material from its namesake project in the Northern Territory. The result, from a caustic conversion and hydrochloric acid leach test, represents a massive leap forward from the 74 per cent MREO extraction achieved in previous conventional leach work and could prove to be a pivotal moment in the company’s mission to develop a processing flowsheet. Barkly Rare Earths is exploring for rare earths and base metals in the Northern Territory. The sighter test - a preliminary small-scale lab test used to check basic assumptions about how an ore will respond to processing - was independently completed by Nagrom in Perth. It was also successful in extracting 94 per cent of the yttrium, a metal used in electronics, high-powered lasers and targeted medical therapies. Importantly, the test separated 92 per cent of the phosphorus impurities into the caustic solution, with no measurable rare earths detected. Removing troublesome elements such as phosphorus early in the process is a significant technical win, as it can simplify and reduce the cost of downstream purification.

Advertisement

‘Achieving 99% MREO extraction to the acid leach solution may unlock the rare earth minerals.’ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright Magnet rare earths, which include neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium, notably making up 34 per cent of the company’s total rare earth oxides basket, are the most sought-after of the 17 rare earth elements. They are critical components in the permanent magnets used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. The metallurgical survey was conducted on a composite sample from Barkly’s flagship Barkly project, which currently hosts a hefty inferred mineral resource of 40 million tonnes at 710 parts per million (ppm) MREO, sitting within a broader halo of 2100 ppm total rare earth oxides (TREO). When considering just how little drilling underpins the existing resource, the sheer scale of the opportunity becomes apparent. The prospect already holds82,000 tonnes of contained TREO, yet the resource was defined from just 46 holes and 755 metres of testing, representing less than one per cent of Barkly’s 5030-square-kilometre project. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “This is an encouraging early metallurgical result for Barkly. Achieving 99% combined MREO extraction to the acid leach solution indicates that caustic conversion may unlock the rare earth minerals ahead of acid leaching while transferring most of the phosphate to a separate conversion-stage solution.”

Advertisement

The global rare earths market has been dominated by China for decades, a situation that has prompted governments and manufacturers in the West to incentivise the development of alternative supply sources. Western nations are now scrambling to secure their own supply chains, with the Australian Government recently committing $1.2 billion to a Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve, primarily for rare earths exploration. With a solid resource already defined, Barkly’s focus is now twofold: to expand the resource and crack the metallurgical code to economically extract the valuable elements. The company is already well into a 10,000-metre drilling campaign across the project, aimed at growing its 40-million-tonne resource by the end of the year. On the processing front, the company says it will now move to confirm the repeatability of its impressive 99 per cent extraction result at a larger scale. Further work will look to optimise the process by tweaking temperature, reagent use and residence times, in addition to evaluating impurity removal and final product recovery. To oversee the crucial next phase of metallurgical work, the company has appointed Lu Zhang of MinPro Consult as an independent consultant. Having only listed on the ASX in January this year after an oversubscribed $8 million IPO, Barkly appears to be moving at pace. With a significant resource in a Tier-1 jurisdiction, a major drilling program underway and now a potentially game-changing metallurgical pathway to follow, the company looks to be assembling the key pieces of the rare earths puzzle.

Advertisement

If the rods keep turning up mineralisation and the metallurgists can replicate this latest result at scale, Barkly might just be rounding the corner at its flagship project at a critical time for the rare earths sector. Thousands of staff at the University of Sydney are set to go on strike on Wednesday, partly over an impasse between workers and management over artificial intelligence. National Tertiary Education Union members will stop work for 24 hours, in a move that is likely to pose major disruptions to the university’s day-to-day operations, as union members hammer out their new enterprise bargaining agreement with management. University of Sydney students are likely to be impacted by Wednesday’s strike. Sam Mooy The union is demanding “provisions to protect staff against any adverse effects of artificial intelligence systems in the workplace,” as well as a 20 per cent pay rise for all staff, and 17 per cent superannuation for casual workers, in a log of claims seen by this masthead. “We want enforceable protections against AI being used to cut jobs, intensify workloads, undermine academic and professional judgement, or replace work and human interaction that are fundamental to a university,” said the NTEU’s Vince Caughley.

Advertisement

“The major concern is the extraordinarily cavalier way this is being approached.” While AI’s impact on students has been well-canvassed, the impact the fledgling technology will have on academic staff has opened a new front. This masthead revealed last month that the state’s universities are deploying AI in lectures, as a virtual assistant for conversational skills and as a “study buddy”. Many across the sector are increasingly worried about the effect it is likely to have on jobs. “There is a real danger that university management has drunk the AI Kool-Aid,” said Caughley. Much of the university will shut for Wednesday, with student or staff ID required to access buildings that day. Almost all of the university’s suitable classes will go online, it said, while labs and other things unable to be done remotely may be cancelled for the day. The University of Sydney reported $1.7 billion in takings from foreign students and recorded a $194 million surplus last financial year, a significant decrease on the surplus of $545 million the previous year.

AI Revealed: The NSW universities using AI in lectures and as ‘study buddies’ A university spokesperson labelled the strike as “premature” and said industrial action would not influence how the new EBA was agreed. “We agree using AI ethically requires a human-centred approach and our Responsible AI Framework, principles and guardrails that govern use have been developed with this as a key value. We also maintain the use of AI is best governed through policies and frameworks that can be updated as needed to respond to this rapidly changing technology, rather than set for the three-year term of the enterprise agreement,” said the spokesperson. “AI is undeniably changing the modern workforce, and we consider it our responsibility to make sure our staff have the opportunities and capabilities they need to drive our research, education and operations.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: No end in sight for 'celeb bait' Facebook ad battle
text:
Australia's consumer watchdog says Meta has no idea what ads it is publishing on its platforms, allowing scammers to profit off fake celebrity endorsements.

The company behind Facebook and Instagram is being sued in the Federal Court for allowing scam cryptocurrency advertisements costing victims at least $100 million.

The 245 ads under fire in the lawsuit featured famous Aussie faces including minerals magnate Andrew 'Twiggy' Forrest and former Sunrise host David Koch.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Using trusted names to flog dodgy financial scams is known as "celebrity bait" and has been supercharged by the use of AI deepfakes.

Mining magnate Andrew Forrest is one of many Australian business figures featured in the scam ads. (Bianca De Marchi/AAP PHOTOS)

Meta, which intends to defend the lawsuit, is accused of not doing enough to stop the proliferation of the scam ads despite knowing they were a problem for years.

Lengthy discussions occurred in the Federal Court on Monday as top silks for the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and Meta battled out which evidence the social media company would be forced to produce.

"Advertising gets itself onto the Facebook platform … without any human ever having reviewed the material," ACCC barrister Naomi Sharp SC said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Meta failed to adopt reasonable safeguards which we say would have reduced the prevalence of the (scam ads)."

However, Meta's barrister argued the consumer watchdog was being unreasonable in its sizeable demands for evidence, including records from internal communications going back years.

"This case is not about every thought that took place within this giant organisation over seven years," Fiona Roughley SC said.

The ACCC lawsuit against Meta was launched in March 2022, but no trial date has been set. (James Ross/AAP PHOTOS)

The ACCC argues its demands for insights from Meta's advertising library will be used to show how lax the company's verification processes were.

"We want to prove a negative ... you can't say what you're publishing on your platform," Ms Sharp said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Ms Sharp also referenced alleged tactics Meta used to stall regulators by cleaning up its Ad Library, as reported by Reuters in December.

"A playbook within Meta designed to dupe regulators around the world, so they can delay for as long as possible verification procedures for advertisers," the ACCC silk said.

Despite the lawsuit being launched in March 2022, no trial date for the case has been set.

Ms Roughley flagged Meta's intention to ask for 12 months to comply with the discovery evidence requests, which will be adjudicated at a later date.
